 First let's create some input. Input size is arbitrary but it is the one used in the automated tests included in the package and to obtain the timings. Here we are assuming a `"hadoop"` backend. By setting `vectorized` to `TRUE` we instruct `keyval` to consider its arguments collections of keys and values, not individual ones. At the same time `to.dfs` automatically switches to a simplified serialization format. The nice thing is that we don't have to remember if a data set was written out with one or the other serialization, as they are compatible on the read side. For testing purposes  we need to create a data set in this format to maximize the benefits of the `vectorized` option.



-  input.size = if(rmr.options.get('backend') == "local") 10^4 else 10^6
-  data = keyval(rep(list(1), input.size),as.list(1:input.size), vectorized = TRUE)
-  input = to.dfs(data)
+  input.size = if(rmr.options.get('backend') == "local") 10^4 else 10^6  data = keyval(rep(list(1), input.size),as.list(1:input.size), vectorized = TRUE)  input = to.dfs(data)



-
-
 ### Read it back
 The simplest possible task is to read back what we just wrote out, and we know how to do that already.

-
 ```r
     from.dfs(input)
 ```

-
-
 In the next code block we switch on vectorization. That is, instead of reading in a list of key-value pairs we are going to have list of vectorized key-value pairs, that is every pair contains a list of keys and a list of values of the same length. The `vectorized` argument can be set to an integer as well for more precise control of how many keys and values should be stored in a key-value pair. With this change alone, from my limited, standalone mode testing we have achieved an almost 7X speed-up (raw timing data is in [`vectorized-API.R`](../tests/vectorized-API.R))

title: do not put inline output in `` for markdown?
description: For R Markdown, the reason to put inline output in ```` is to prevent unescaped special characters (everything inside ```` will be interpreted as-is), and the way to get rid of this is to use `I()`. We can change it: if you want backticks, you can write ```r x```, i.e. an extra pair of backticks around ``r x``, otherwise the inline hook will write normal text into the output for inline R code.

description:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/11609131/r-markdown-equivalent-in-sas

I do not use SAS but whoever do are welcome to contribute to https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/R/engine.R

Again, it is nothing a call `system('sas code.sas -print label.log')`, but it might be slightly more complicated than other languages because of the old-fashioned "log-and-output-everything" nature of SAS. Even you just say hello world, you may get 30 lines of output in which only 1 line is useful. There might be options to suppress the proud logs, though.

The design of `knitr` has taken care of some gory details in SASweave (http://homepage.cs.uiowa.edu/~rlenth/SASweave/), and two challenges remain:
- clean up the text output
- how to deal with graphics output (well, who cares...)

In the end we can write code chunks like this

``` sas
<<engine='sas'>>=
data _null_;
put 'Hello, world!';
run;
@
```

title: cache=TRUE and load("file.Rdata") [feat.suggestion]
description:
# Feature suggestion:

Currently _cache=TRUE_ does not work properly with the _load_ function:

I would expect that when running a chunk with a load("afile.Rdata") command, knit would use the cache only if "afile.Rdata" has not changed since the cache was built.
However, knit always uses the cache if it is available.
# Example:

Please run the example twice, and change the "a" value on the second run to check that knit is using the cache instead of reloading testcache.Rdata.
## Original source: test.Rmd

``````
    # Set *a* to a value (change the value on a second run):
    ```{r chunk1,cache=FALSE}
    a <- 7
    ```

    # Save *a* to a file and remove it from workspace:
    ```{r chunk2,cache=FALSE,dependson=c("chunk1")}
    message("A exists? ",exists("a"))
    save("a",file="testcache.Rdata")
    rm(a)
    message("A exists? ",exists("a"))
    ```

    # Load the variable
    ```{r chunk3,cache=TRUE}
    load("testcache.Rdata")
    ```

    # Print the stored value

    ```{r chunk4,cache=TRUE,dependson=c("chunk3")}
    print(a)
    ```
``````
## First run (fragment):

``````
    # Set *a* to a value (change the value on a second run):
    ```r
    a <- 7
    ```
    # Print the stored value
    ```r
    print(a)
    ```

    ```
    ## [1] 7
    ```
``````
## Second run (fragment):

``````
    # Set *a* to a value (change the value on a second run):
    ```r
    a <- 8
    ```

    # Print the stored value
    ```r
    print(a)
    ```

    ```
    ## [1] 7
    ```
``````

Notice how _a_ is taken from the cache instead of loaded from "testcache.Rdata", even though "testcache.Rdata" has been modified.
# Possible solution:

When we reach chunk3:
- When generating the cache, include an md5sum (or a timestamp) of "testcache.Rdata"
- When using the cache, check if the cached md5sum matches the actual md5sum of the file and regenerate the whole chunk if they don't match.
# Difficulty:

I don't know much about knitr, but depending on how it is designed it may be hard to detect a _load_ function inside a chunk and it may be hard to check for md5sums to decide if the cache has to be updated.

If there is anything I can do to help, please feel free to comment on this issue. I am not an R expert, but given the right hints I could try to work on a patch.

title: Bundle external functions into a separate package `knitrExtra`
description:
This is more of a suggestion than an issue. As much as I enjoy all the extra functionality being added to `knitr` every day, I believe that lot of the extra functionality are tangential to the purpose of `knitr`. Over time, this can add a lot of bloat to the code base of `knitr` and make it increasingly difficult to maintain error-free.

My suggestion is to rethink the structure of the package, and bundle the extras as `knitrExtra`. This would make it easy to add features to `knitr` without really modifying the core.

title: reversible knitting
description:
I've been contemplating a project of integrating an online wiki, such as that provided by github or googlecode, with an R package. The idea would be to have:
- a ./inst/wiki directory in the package, containing some form of noweb source files mixing R code with a lightweight markup, say GFM.
- upon R CMD check, or some other operation, the files are knit, producing figures etc.
- a function uploads the updated files to the online wiki.

Thus, the online wiki contains reproducible examples, and the package documentation can be improved/extended by a number of casual users online.

One major hurdle here is the reverse process: suppose a user modifies the wiki page _online_; how do we synchronize the changes with the local version? It is easy to synchronise the output file, but how does one extract the changes and apply them to the original noweb source file? 

I imagine this might involve adding the name of the original code chunks as comments in the output files. 

Any thoughts on this framework?

title: Improve documentation of output argument to knit2pdf
description:
In `knit2pdf`, the documentation of the `output` argument says

This contrasts with `knit2HTML` where `output` is passed on to `markdown::markdonwToHTML` where it is the output HTML file. (Or so it seems; I've not used `knit2HTML`.)

title: pandoc options parsing broken for multiple variables
description:
In the `pandoc` function, you use `read.dcf(con)` to parse options for pandoc, without specifying the `all = TRUE` option.

When using multiple "variable" tags, this leads to only one (the last) variable being passed to pandoc, which uses variables quite extensively for template customizations. 

I am aware that changing this requires changes that go beyond only adding `all = TRUE` to read.dcf as you'd probably have to split the value into separate entities etc.

title: Protection against missing files when setting the theme
description:
In knit_theme$set, if the theme is a file that doesn't exist, you get the obscure error message

```
##Error in end.lines[sapply(dec.lines, function(x) which.min(end.lines <  :
##  invalid subscript type 'list'
```

The problem lies in `theme_to_header_latex` and `theme_to_header_html`.  If the file doesn't exist, `knitr` assumes that you are looking for a them that ships with the package.  It doesn't find one, but `system.file` returns a empty wtring instead of throwing an error, and the problem is buried until later, when it is hard to trace back to the cause.

 Adding `mustWork = TRUE` to the call to `system.file` should make the source of the problem clearer.

```
css_file = if (file.exists(theme))
    theme
else {
    system.file("themes", sprintf("%s.css", theme), package = "knitr", mustWork = TRUE)
}
```

`css.parser`, where the error is currently thrown from, doesn't behave well when the input is empty.  I suggest adding the line 

```
if(length(dec.lines) == 0) return(character())
```

after the point where `dec.lines` is defined.

title: Add timestamp to logfile (at least in verbose mode)
description:
Knitr + caching works wonderfully when running very large jobs on remote servers, where jobs can't be run interactively but are submitted to a queue.  For profiling purposes it would be super convenient if the log files included the timestamp when each chunk was run.

title: should knitr check dev exists before looking for extension?
description:
If i have the following chunk header:

Error: cannot find appropriate filename extensions for device eps;

This makes me think that the device `eps` exists, when in fact it does not. If I add `fix.ext='eps'`, then knitr gives the following error:

Error in get(dev, mode = "function") : 
object 'eps' of mode 'function' was not found

Should this error also be displayed in the first case? It might be even more user-friendly if knitr appended/prepended something like "device 'eps' not valid".

error: the device 'eps' does not exist.

postscript, cairo_ps, CairoPS, Cairo_ps

description:
The current [regexp based highlighter](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/R/highlight.R) is certainly not reliable, e.g.

``` r
tableplot(diamonds, pals = list("Set1(7)", "Set5", rainbow(8)))

`Set1` will be recognized as a function, which should be a character string in this context.

In theory we can make a code walker with the `codetools` package to walk though the code, check the leaves (are they functions? constants? ...) and highlight them accordingly. title: Suggestion for default handling of errors
description:
I understand that the current default is not to stop on errors and to show the error message if one occurs in a chunk.
I would suggest the following defaults, which I think would make users' life easier -- and safer:
- default chunk behaviour: stop on error **and** show error message in **both** the ouput chunk and the (console-)log, with details of the chunk code where the error occured. This is because generally the user expects his code to run without errors and wants to know when one occurs, without having to specify:

``` r
opts_knit$set(progress = TRUE, verbose = FALSE, stop_on_error = 2L)
```
- In some cases, the user expect an error to occur and in fact wants to show the reader the expected error message. This could be achieved when explicitly specifying the chook option `error=TRUE`, i.e. it tells knit "it's ok, I know this chunk will throw an error, show it to me and continue".
  - If the global default behaviour is switched to "don't stop on errors", then the effect of option `error` is reversed: chunks with `error=TRUE` will stop and show the error in both the document and log.

I am sure there are issues with this, one would possibly need another chunk option to separate "stop on error" and "show errors". In all cases, errors should by default be shown in the (console-)log, otherwise one really feels one cannot trust everything went well in the knitting.

Thanks

title: change the meaning of error/message/warning=TRUE/FALSE
description:
- `TRUE`: capture and show it
- `FALSE`: do not capture it in `evaluate()`

this will require a change to the `evaluate` package: `evaluate(..., warning = TRUE, message = TRUE)`

this will make it easier to define the behavior of messages; the `stop_on_error` option is kind of awkward (who cares about 0, 1, 2?)

title: Integration of Roger Peng's `cacher` and `cachesweave` packages?
description:
Maybe you are already familiar with Roger's `cacher` package (e.g. see the [paper](http://www.jstatsoft.org/v26/i07/paper) published in the R journal (is also the vignette of course)?  It looks like a more sophisticated approach to caching -- each line gets a SHA-1 hash so we can differentiate between otherwise identical calls, reconstruct the order of calls, etc.  It seems to go a long way towards more reproducible runs than the standard Sweave approach (e.g. see this [stats.stackechange question](http://t.co/uUJxVRzq).  Also seems geared at creating the "research compendium" R package.  

Anyway, if you haven't seen it I thought it would be of interest; I'm sure you'll be able to understand it better than me.  Just the spirit of this sounded very apropos for knitr.

title: Separate R execution from LaTeX compilation (or: How to write a hook that surrounds all chunk output by \newcommand{\chunkname}{...}?)
description:
By now I have completed two papers using knitr. The tool is amazing, but when doing the final writeup (and thus working _mostly_, but not entirely, inside LaTeX), it slows me down a lot, and I am looking for ways to speed this particular stage.

The caching feature helps, but not always. Minor changes to a chunk on which many other chunks depend requires the whole analysis to run again, and this sometimes takes hours. (No kidding.) I am looking for a way to separate the compilation of the LaTeX document (which can be usually done in seconds) from the actual analysis.

My first idea was to create an .Rnw file that would define, for every chunk, one LaTeX macro that contains its result:

```
<<testchunk,as.cmd=TRUE>>=
a <- 1
@
```

would become

```
\newcommand{\testchunk}{%
... a <- 1 ...
}
```

I have tried to achieve this with hooks, but no luck so far. Neither chunk nor output hooks will let me put the required `\newcommand` outside the surrounding `knitrout` environment.

But then it occurred to me that the main issue is that knitr waits for writing the LaTeX file until the analysis is finished. Why not writing it just after every chunk, with placeholders for the chunks that have not been computed yet? (Preferably first writing to a temporary file in the same directory, and just renaming after the file has been written.) Writing the .tex file should be cheap, and could be made a global option, too. What do you think? I could even give it a try myself, if you could provide me with a pointer where to start.

title: Issue with tidy=TRUE and a multi-line character string
description:
Using the `lavaan` package, you specify structural equation models as long strings. I noticed that the following code block raised an error in knitr 0.6.3.

``````
```{r tidy=TRUE}
library(lavaan)
Data <- PoliticalDemocracy
m1_model <- '
# measurement model
ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

# regressions
dem60 ~ ind60
dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
'

m1_fit <- sem(m1_model, data=Data)
```
``````

It produces the following error:

```
 ## Error: 1:83: unexpected symbol 1: ~
 ## y5+y6+y7+y8invisible(".BeGiN_TiDy_IdEnTiFiEr_HaHaHa.HaHaHa_EnD_TiDy_IdEnTiFiEr")invisible
 ## ^
```

Using `tidy=FALSE` resolves the problem. 
I wasn't sure whether this problem is known and that the standard procedure is just to turn off tidy, or whether it's a useful challenging test  for tidy to try to pass.

Obviously in this situation, I would want to turn off tidy, but I imagine if tidy truly does get confused, it might be better for it just to print R source code as is and perhaps throw a warning in the log.

title: Strange behavior with figures
description:
I get strange behavior with figures. In some chunks knitr generates two figures from a single plot function, and the figures generated from 'chunkname' are named 'chunkname1.pdf' and 'chunkname2.pdf'. Sometimes, the first one is just a blank figure of the same size as the second one, and sometimes it is a file which cannot be open. As a work around, I set the `fig.keep='last'` option. But now I would like to display two plots from a same chunk and setting `fig.keep` to its default value, knitr generates 3 PDF figure files with the first one a corrupted file (one which can not be open).

I have knitr version 1.2 (2013-04-10), R 3.0.0 64bit (r62697 2013-04-30) under Win7 64. Here are the settings I am using:

```
knit_hooks$set(par = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) par(mar = c(4, 4, .1, .1))
})

opts_knit$set(concordance=TRUE, self.contained=TRUE)

opts_chunk$set(fig.path="figSW/SW-", keep.source=FALSE, 
   verbose=TRUE,  message=FALSE)
```

title: Barplots in loop preceeded by barplot only outputs final barplot
description:
If I have a barplot call, followed by a loop containing more barplot calls, I will see the first (non-loop) barplot, and then the final loop barplot. This problem also ignores the fig.keep chunk option.

If I have a loop containing barplots, but first display another kind of plot (scatterplot, etc.) then the loop works fine.

```
sessionInfo()
## R version 3.0.1 (2013-05-16)
## Platform: i386-w64-mingw32/i386 (32-bit)
## 
## locale:
## [1] LC_COLLATE=English_United States.1252 
## [2] LC_CTYPE=English_United States.1252   
## [3] LC_MONETARY=English_United States.1252
## [4] LC_NUMERIC=C                          
## [5] LC_TIME=English_United States.1252    
## 
## attached base packages:
## [1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base     
## 
## other attached packages:
## [1] knitr_1.2
## 
## loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
## [1] digest_0.6.3   evaluate_0.4.4 formatR_0.8    stringr_0.6.2 
## [5] tools_3.0.1
```

I have reduced my problem down to the following Rmd script:

``````
Barplots Example
----------------------------
First we display a barplot, and then barplots in a loop. Only the final loop barplot is seen.
```{r Broken}

barplot(table(mtcars$mpg), main="All")

#Barplots in a loop will only display final plot.
for (numcyl in levels(as.factor(mtcars$cyl))) {
  barplot(table(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl==numcyl]), main=paste(numcyl, "but where are 4 and 6?"))
}
```
This time, we first plot *any other kind of plot*. The looped barplots work fine.

```{r Works}
plot(table(mtcars$mpg), main="All")
#plot(mtcars$mpg, main="All")

#Works
for (numcyl in levels(as.factor(mtcars$cyl))) {
 barplot(table(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl==numcyl]), main=paste(numcyl, "loop after other plot"))
}
```

Also, just plotting a bunch of barplots without a loop is fine.

```{r Works2}
#Works:
barplot(table(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl=="4"]), main="4 no loop")
barplot(table(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl=="6"]), main="6 no loop")
barplot(table(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl=="8"]), main="8 no loop")

```
Since we displayed a barplot in the previous chunk, we will only see the final plot here:
```{r StillBroken}
for (numcyl in levels(as.factor(mtcars$cyl))) {
 barplot(table(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl==numcyl]), main=paste(numcyl, "stillbroken"))
}

```
But what if we tell knitr we want to keep all of the plots?

```{r FigKeepBrokenToo, fig.keep='all'}

barplot(table(mtcars$mpg), main="All")

#Barplots in a loop will only display final plot.
for (numcyl in levels(as.factor(mtcars$cyl))) {
  barplot(table(mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl==numcyl]), main=paste(numcyl, "fig.keep ignored"))
}
```
So there you have it.
```{r session-info, cache=FALSE}
sessionInfo()
Sys.time()
```
``````

title: knitr vs. interactive R behaviour
description:
I am a bit puzzle with a .Rmd file that I can proceed line by line in an interactive R session, and also with `R CMD BATCH`, but that fails when using `knit("test.Rmd")`. I am not sure where the problem lies, and I tried to narrow the problem down as much as I could. Here is the example (in `test.Rmd`):

``````
```{r Rinit, include = FALSE, cache = FALSE}
opts_knit$set(stop_on_error = 2L)
library(adehabitatLT)
```

The functions to be used later:

```{r functions}
ld <- function(ltraj) {
    if (!inherits(ltraj, "ltraj")) 
        stop("ltraj should be of class ltraj")
    inf <- infolocs(ltraj)
    df <- data.frame(
        x = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$x)),
        y = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$y)),
        date = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$date)),
        dx = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$dx)),
        dy = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$dy)),
        dist = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$dist)),
        dt = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$dt)),
        R2n = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$R2n)),
        abs.angle = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$abs.angle)),
        rel.angle = unlist(lapply(ltraj, function(x) x$rel.angle)),
        id = rep(id(ltraj), sapply(ltraj, nrow)),
        burst = rep(burst(ltraj), sapply(ltraj, nrow)))
    class(df$date) <- c("POSIXct", "POSIXt")
    attr(df$date, "tzone") <- attr(ltraj[[1]]$date, "tzone")
    if (!is.null(inf)) {
        nc <- ncol(inf[[1]])
        infdf <- as.data.frame(matrix(nrow = nrow(df), ncol = nc))
        names(infdf) <- names(inf[[1]])
        for (i in 1:nc) infdf[[i]] <- unlist(lapply(inf, function(x) x[[i]]))
        df <- cbind(df, infdf)
    }
    return(df)
}
ltraj2sldf <- function(ltr, proj4string = CRS(as.character(NA))) {
    if (!inherits(ltr, "ltraj")) 
        stop("ltr should be of class ltraj")
    df <- ld(ltr)
    df <- subset(df, !is.na(dist))
    coords <- data.frame(df[, c("x", "y", "dx", "dy")], id = as.numeric(row.names(df)))
    res <- apply(coords, 1, function(dfi) Lines(Line(matrix(c(dfi["x"], 
        dfi["y"], dfi["x"] + dfi["dx"], dfi["y"] + dfi["dy"]), 
        ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)), ID = format(dfi["id"], scientific = FALSE)))
    res <- SpatialLinesDataFrame(SpatialLines(res, proj4string = proj4string), 
        data = df)
    return(res)
}
```

I load the object and apply the `ltraj2sldf` function:

```{r fail}
load("tr.RData")
juvStp <- ltraj2sldf(trajjuv, proj4string = CRS("+init=epsg:32617"))
dim(juvStp)
```
``````

Using `knitr("test.Rmd")` fails with:

```
label: fail
Quitting from lines 66-75 (test.Rmd) 
Error in SpatialLinesDataFrame(SpatialLines(res, proj4string = 
proj4string),  (from     <text>#32) : 
  row.names of data and Lines IDs do not match
```

Using the call directly in the R console after the error occurred works as expected...

The problem is related to the way `format` produces the ID (in the `apply` call of `ltraj2sldf`), just before ID 100,000: using an interactive call, R gives "99994", "99995", "99996", "99997", "99998", "99999", "100000"; using knitr R gives "99994", " 99995", " 99996", " 99997", " 99998", " 99999", "100000", with additional leading spaces.

Is there any reason for this behaviour to occur? Why should `knitr` behave differently than a direct call in R? I have to admit I'm having hard time with that one, since I cannot debug it (it works in an interactive session)!

Any hint will be much appreciated. Of course, I can provide the .RData if it helps (the file is 4.5 Mo).
Sincerely,
Mathieu Basille.

The [documentation states](http://yihui.name/knitr/objects):

> It is recommended to get the settings done in the first chunk with cache = FALSE and include = FALSE like this (we may call this chunk as the configuration chunk):

However, this is not exactly correct. I spent an hour or two looking into this. The following will produce an error:

``````
```{r}
opts_knit$set(
    root.dir = dirname(getwd())
    );
source('lib/lib.R');
```
``````

yields

```
## Warning: cannot open file 'lib/lib.R': No such file or directory
## Error: cannot open the connection
```

However, moving `source()` to the next chunk works fine:

``````
```{r}
opts_knit$set(
    root.dir = dirname(getwd())
    );
```

```{r}
source('lib/lib.R');
```
``````

This seems to be the case for both `Rmd` and `Rnw` sources.

The documentation should therefore read:

> Knitr's settings _must_ be set in the first chunk with cache = FALSE and include = FALSE like this (we may call this chunk as the configuration chunk):

title: Default for root.url
description:
I think the default for `root.url` should be specified based on the `outputFile`. Here is my rationale.

**Case 1. Run from Rmd Directory**

This works because the `md` file is also generated in the same directory and all assets are correctly linked.

```
knit('test.Rmd')
```

**Case 2. Run from a Different Working Directory, No Output Specified.**

This works too because by default the output is generated in the current working directory and hence all assets are correctly linked.

```
knit('root/test.Rmd')
```

**Case 3. Run from Different Working Directory, Output Specified**

This fails to link assets correctly, since code chunks are still run from the 'root' directory. I know it can be easily tweaked by sticking an `opts_knit$set(root.url = 'root')` in the Rmd file, but I think it should be the default.

```
knit('root/test.Rmd', 'root/test.md')
```

IMPLEMENTATION:

One way to implement it is to determine the relative path from the current working directory to the output file directory, and set it as `root.url`.

title: tables() from data.table
description:
I've noticed some issues in other posts about data.table and environments and stumbled upon an one of my own.  The tables() argument depends on the environment and works fine if it is in the same chunk as where the data.table was created, but if it is in its own chunk it will not work.  This has something to do with caching as setting `cache=FALSE` takes care of the issue.  It does not, however, affect just accessing the tables.  A reproducible example is below.
# data.table issue

``` r settings
opts_chunk$set(cache=TRUE,cache.path="dtCache/")
```

If we call tables() in the same chunk where the tables were created it works, if we call it in its own chunk it does not work.

``` r build-datatable
require(data.table)
theDT <- data.table(A=1:10, B=letters[1:10], C=LETTERS[11:20])
theDT
nrow(theDT)
carsDT <- data.table(cars)
head(carsDT)
nrow(carsDT)
tables()
```

Now we look at the tables command in its own chunk.

``` r show-tables,dependson='build-datatable'
tables()
```

Here tables will only recognize the tables from this chunk and not the previous ones.

``` r more-dt,dependson='build-datatable'
secondDT <- data.table(First=10:1, Second=1:10)
secondDT
tables()
```

We can still access all the previous data.tables though.

``` r get-other-dts
theDT
secondDT
head(carsDT)
```

If you turn off caching, everything works fine.

Sorry that GitHub is incorrectly interpreting the code but pasting all of it into a Rmd file should make things clear.

title: selectively include output of a chunk?
description:
Hi,

I've been using the very handy externalization feature of `knitr`, where I can conveniently develop the R code, and when it's polished insert the relevant bits inside a Rnw document. A common problem I face is the following: say my analysis is split into a few steps,

1- (lengthy / messy) definition of some functions [ _don't show in final report_ ]

2- call to the function [ _show in final report_ ]

3- (messy / lengthy) creation of the plot using ggplot2 [ _don't show in final report_ ]

4- printing the plot [ _only show the plot in the final report, not the `print(p)` statement_ ]

In the final report, I often find I don't want to overwhelm the reader (me, in fact) with technical details such as (1) and (3). In the current workflow, this means that I'll have to split this into 4 chunks, even though it's really the same part of the study. Further, I need to worry about setting echo=T/F, include=T/F, dependson= for each of these 4 chunks.

I wonder if this could be simplified somehow, by allowing one of two things:
- have the option show no _text_ output, but still print _plots_ (meaning I can keep steps 3 and 4 in the same chunk)
- provide an internal keyword in the form of R comments that defines lines that may be exluded from the echoed code. Something along those lines:

``` r
##@knitr messychunk

##@hide
foo = function(...){

## ...

}

##@show
result <- lapply(1:10, foo)
summary(result)

plot(result)

##@hide
p <- ggplot(result) +
 ## ....

##@show
p
```

title: Group joiners
description:
Following up #625, I think the following is reasonable to simplify the implementation of #620 and also create an easier to read output:
- In `output.R::process_file`, make `res` a list instead of a character vector
- `process_group` (and perhaps `process_tangle`, too) returns an object with attributes
- These attributes tell how this group needs to be joined with the preceding _and_ following group. Options are
  - Blank line
  - Space
  - Non-breakable space
  - Glued
- A "stronger" join takes precedence

Chances to introduce regressions are minor thanks to CI :-)

title: Integrate with fixme package
description:
The [fixme LaTeX package](http://www.ctan.org/pkg/fixme) offers a way to annotate LaTeX code with errors and warnings which also can be collected and printed in a list. If each R warning/error emits a `\knitwarning` or `\kniterror` command, the user will be made more aware of issues in the code. These could be emitted even if printing of warnings is disabled.

The package is very mature, but has also received updates recently. It is superior to the competitors `todonotes` (much faster because no `tikz` is used) and `fixmetodonotes` (more mature, more presentation options, nicer output).

register_stitch_handler(class, output.format, handler.function)

title: kable chokes on table with NAs -- something to do with padding
Folder name with spaces gives an error in v1.5, but not in v1.4
description:
Since v1.5 knitr sanitises folders with spaces, e.g (on Windows 7, RStudio 0.98.310) for:

```
D:\folder with spaces\RStudio_project_without_spaces\figures\figure_name_without_spaces
```

One gets the error:

```
`Warning in (if (out_format(c("latex", "sweave", "listings", "markdown"))) sanitize_fn else str_c)(path,  :
  replaced special characters in figure filename "D:\folder with spaces\RStudio_project_without_spaces\figures\figure_name_without_spaces" ->` etc
```

I guess this has to do with this cran NEWS item for v1.3.

```
  *- for Markdown output, the figure filenames no longer allow special
  characters like spaces, and special characters will be automatically
  replaced by `_`; this change will avoid problems when publishing to RPubs
  from RStudio: if figure paths contain special characters, the figures will
  not be uploaded (thanks, Sangsoon Woo)*
```

But in versions 1.3 and 1.4 a folder name with a space below the project folder was no problem. I also guess this lower level folder name will not be used when uploading to RPubs.

Is this an accident, or does knitr as of v1.5 officially not support directory names with spaces anymore?

**EDIT**: Found the cause after installing v1.4.1. The new knitr writes the full path name in a figure link, the old one only the relative name:

```
![Figure A](figures/figa.png)
```

vs:

```
![Figure A](D:/somepath/someproject/figures/figa.png)
```

I changed my directory name to something without spaces, but unfortunately, now `pandoc` has problems with the new format:

Further tests with `pandoc`:

```
![Figure A](file://D:/somepath/someproject/figures/figa.png)
```

Does not work.

```
![Figure A](D:\\somepath\\someproject\\figures\\figa.png)
```

_Does_ work.

print.fx=function(x)
{

  return(NULL)
}

class(x)="fx"
x

print.fx=function(x)
{

  return(NULL)

print.fx=function(x)
{

  invisible()
}

title: knitr::pandoc can't create pdf and tex files with a single config
description:
Hi Yihui

I'd like to use the 'knitr::pandoc' function to create both pdf and latex outputs. Unfortunately it seems this cannot be done in a single call the way the function is currently structured, since the function requires a unique "t" for each target output, while both pdf and latex outputs are of type 'latex', and differ only by their output argument:

``` dcf
t: latex
bibliography: components/references.bib
output: manuscript.pdf

t: latex
bibliography: components/references.bib
output: manuscript.tex
```

I'd like to do something like 

``` coffee
pandoc(file, format=c("pdf", "latex"), config="config.txt")
```

which obviously doesn't work in the current system.  The only work-around I can see is to use 2 different calls to `pandoc` relying on different config files.  This is a common use-case for me since I generally need both the tex and pdf.  

Anyway, I'd appreciate any solution or your insight on how to go about this.  I usually just leave all this up to calls in Makefiles, but as I work with collaborators I've hit problems where Makefiles behave differently on different platforms, so it seemed desirable to use the internal knitr function instead. I haven't convinced myself that this is in fact wiser than just using Makefiles, so I'd love to hear your thoughts on what exactly the motivation is for including the `pandoc` function in `knitr` in the first place, and if use case is not a good fit for it.  

Thanks so much, as always,

Carl

title: Incorrect continuation prompt when using render_sweave() with not-evaluated chunk
description:
When I use render_sweave() to get back Sweave style for code chunk.  If there is a statement across multiple line, the "+" continuation prompt will be replaced by ">".  For example, when you compile the Rnw file below:

```
\documentclass[a4paper]{article}

\title{Knitr And Sweave Example}
\author{Simon}

<<<setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE>>=
require(knitr)
opts_chunk$set(tidy=FALSE)
opts_chunk$set(prompt=TRUE)
render_sweave(); opts_chunk$set(eval=FALSE)
@

\begin{document}

\maketitle

In this example we show the results when using knitr to give Sweave style outputs, with a single R statement across multiple line being not evaluated:

<<>>=
set.seed(19)
a <- sample(1:1000,
            5)
a
@


\end{document}
```

The following text will be shown in the the final PDF file:

```
> set.seed(19)
> a <- sample(1:1000,
>             5)
> a
```

However, the correct text should be:

```
> set.seed(19)
> a <- sample(1:1000,
+             5)
> a
```

title: Inline code chunks, tangle, and R CMD check errors
description:
It seems that R CMD check has decided to tangle knitr vignettes and source the resulting `.R` script as way of checking the R code even when `--no-build-vignettes` is selected.  

This can create a problem since `tangle` ignores the inline chunks, and yet inline chunks can modify the R code.  As a consequence it is possible to have a vignette that compiles perfectly fine when knit directly, but does not execute successfully when `tangle`'d and then `source`'d. 

 (Yes, I realize they are primarily designed for just echoing values, not setting them, but for instance, in `knitcitations` my inline calls to things like `citep` change an environmental variable).  

Perhaps tangle should not ignore inline blocks?

title: summary() function gives strange results when used in knitr
description:
I'm currently trying to use summary for a small analysis project, but I noticed it is giving incorrect results. 

Take this data for example:

```
years <- c(2000, 2001, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2012, 2012, 2012, 2012)
```

If I run it in the R console I get:

```
> summary(biopsy.years)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   2000    2004    2008    2007    2012    2012 
```

If I run it in knitr I get:

```
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    2000    2000    2010    2010    2010    2010
```

I found an answer on StackOverflow. For some reason setting:

```
options(digits=7)
```

in a chunk at the beginning of the Rmd file fixes it. I have no idea what it does, just that digits = 7 is the R default.

[Here's the SO link as well.](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/14811077/summary-function-gives-strange-results-with-knitr-rstudio)

title: read_chunk without label does not increment chunk_counter
description:
If using read_chunk and do not set the label, 

if (any(idx <- !nzchar(labels))) labels[idx] = unnamed_chunk(seq_len(sum(idx)))

Even though this will give an unnamed-chunk-n, it will not increment the chunk_counter. If you attempt to output any other label-less chunk after this, the label will conflict and fail will duplicate label.

For example, a call to knit_child where the child has chunks with no labels or read_chunk without label will fail. Or, simply a label-less chunk inline.

processing file: ./da-numeric.Rmd
Quitting from lines NA-46 (./da-numeric.Rmd)
Error in parse_block(g, patterns) : duplicate label 'unnamed-chunk-1'
Calls: knit ... process_file -> split_file -> lapply -> FUN -> parse_block

title: "SSL certificate problem" with imgur_upload
description:
I'm using `opts_knit$set(upload.fun = imgur_upload)` and getting the standard SSL certificate error, which you should be able to solve by adding `cainfo = system.file("CurlSSL", "cacert.pem", package = "RCurl")` to the `RCurl::postForm` call.

I think this originates from when you switched to v3 of the imgur API here: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/commit/d5bd8d98b4699ee68635bf4ab3d57baaf816b138

I'm surprised no one else has had this problem, though.

title: Caching Rcpp Chunks
description:
I am having trouble with the caching of chunks that have Rcpp code. Let's say a C++ function is properly built in chunk1 and successfully called in chunk2 and the file is knitted. Then the function is called again from chunk3, however, this time there's an error: "## Error: could not find function "fibonacci"" This seems like a caching issue. The problem is seen below taken from https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/029-engine-Rcpp.md # Call Rcpp from knitr 
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
opts_chunk$set(cache = TRUE) # because the compilation takes time, let's cache it
```
When the chunk option `engine='Rcpp'` is specified, the code chunk will be compiled through **Rcpp** via `sourceCpp()`: Test for `fibonacci`: 
```{r fibCpp, engine='Rcpp'}
#include 

// [[Rcpp::export]]
int fibonacci(const int x) {
    if (x == 0 || x == 1) return(x);
    return (fibonacci(x - 1)) + fibonacci(x - 2);
}
```
Because `fibonacci` was defined with the `Rcpp::export` attribute it can now be called as a normal R function: 
 
```{r fibTest, dependson='fibCpp'}
fibonacci(10L)
fibonacci(20L)
```
If the file is now knitted everything works fine. But if the above chunk is modified, it has to be rebuild and it generates the error. The same error occurs if a new chunk that calls `fibonacci` is written. It appears to be an issue with caching. I am using knitr 1.2.5 installed from GitHub today and Rcpp 0.10.3.

title: Too aggressive purge of cache
description:
The following code never uses cached results:

``` s
library(knitr)
knit(output='test.tex', text='
<<conf, cache=FALSE>>=
opts_knit$set(verbose=TRUE)
opts_chunk$set(cache=TRUE, autodep=TRUE)
@
<<chunk1_prep>>=
x <- 1
@
<<chunk1>>=
x
@
')
```

I think every time knitr gets to `chunk1`, it removes cache for `chunk1_prep` because of the following code (only hash tags should be allowed after `_`):

``` s
purge_cache = function(options) {
  # purge my old cache and cache of chunks dependent on me
  cache$purge(paste(valid_path(
    options$cache.path, c(options$label, dep_list$get(options$label))
  ), '_*', sep = ''))
}
```

title: Chunk labels that have prefix matches are not cached.
description:
When there are two chunks, one of which has a label that is a prefix match of another, the chunk with the longer label will not be cached.  For example, if there are chunks named plot_data and plot and both have cache=TRUE, the plot_data chunk will not be cached.

This gist demonstrates the problem: https://gist.github.com/jrauser/3d2e753de1fb65731a38.  Compile it and look in the cache directory.  There will be no file for the plot_data chunk.

title: code "tidying" issues when using selective code evaluation
description:
Sometimes I use multiple comment lines in a row:

``````
````{r eval=c(1:2, 4)}
# don't evaluate
# the next line
rnorm(1000000000)
# was it evaluated?
````
``````

If I use `tidy=FALSE`, everything is good and the output looks like

```
# don't evaluate
# the next line
## rnorm(1000000000)
# was it evaluated?
```

But if I use `tidy=TRUE`, I might get

```

# was it evaluated?
```

Which wouldn't be a big deal, except the `eval` specification is applied AFTER code tidying, so the line that was not meant to be run actually gets run.

The `eval` specification should consider the line breaks in the original code, not the tidied code. Is this possible?

title: Using opts_current$get within a chunk option returns the previous chunk's options
description:
If `opts_current$get` is called by another chunk option, the options of the previous chunk are returned instead. I am guessing this happens because `opts_current` is updated after all the chunk options are evaluated. 

I think it would be better if `opts_current` entries were updated sequentially, in the order the user specifies the options in the chunk header. That would allow users to use the current chunk options in another chunk option, as long as they had defined those options first.

There may be issues with my suggestion, but it still seems buggy that you can refer a _previous_ chunk's options using `opts_current`. I think that `opts_current` should at a minimum be reset to `opts_chunk` at the conclusion of each chunk.

title: Exclude chunk label from digest/hash calculation (?)
description:
Hi Yihui,

My guess is that this has come up before and is not implemented for a reason, but I couldn't find any info on it.

I can think of a few motivations for this. First, one might simply want to change label to make them more clear. Second, if the order of unnamed chunks is changed, the labels will also be changed. Third, I haven't tested this but I wonder if with child documents when the children are run by themselves the numbering of unnamed chunks starts from 0 but when run in the parent the numbering is wherever they are placed. This could be confusing to users. Fourth, if the chunks have the same contents (and thus MD5 sums), should they share the same cache data?

Should the label be part of the calculated digest? If not, this is an easy fix of adding 'label' to `cache0.opts`.

Another question is: should the label be part of the hash? Is it there only for convenience (if someone wants to directly access the underlying cache objects)? For example, Git does not care about filenames. Why should knitr care about labels? If you do want to keep the label as part of the hash, then the hash lookup is a little more complicated. Currently it is nice and simple, you just have to check whether the path exists. If you want to match against the MD5, you would have to loop through all the RData files in cache.path, parse the MD5 out and check whether it matches. I'm happy to do this work, but I don't know if you want this extra complication.

title: Print matrices as tables by default
description:
Currently, matrices printed from R code result in text output in the resulting document. For example, `matrix(1:10, 2, 5)` gives

```
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
[1,]    1    3    5    7    9
[2,]    2    4    6    8   10
```

This is not optimal since it only looks right with fixed-width fonts, and cannot be copied to e.g. a text editor or a spreadsheet application. In one word: it's in an unstructured, useless format.

One of the current situations is to use `print(xtable(...), type="html")` in a `results="asis"` chunk. This works great, but requires additional code, while I think this behavior should be the default. Tables are not required to look incredible by default, but at least they should be tables, with a minimally correct formatting (e.g. row/column names in bold, which is not possible in the R console but makes things much easier to read in a real document). There could be an option to disable this behavior, but I think everybody would gain from getting clean tables out of the box.

My use case (but there are many others) is that I'm using RStudio with students, and I would like to tell them to use knitr to create reproducible HTML reports from where they can copy their tables. It would be much more convenient to avoid the xtable trick.

Implementation-wise, I'm not sure how you'd do this, but the R2HTML package already has some support for this kind of things after HTMLStart() is called. I guess you merely need to replace the `print.matrix()`, but you know better than I do.

Thanks for this very nice package!

title: Report writing workflow: decouple steps of writing of code and document.
description:
Rnw/Rmd is a great format for reproducible reports. However I think the current workflow of writing such reports is not optimal. When writing (non-reproducible) reports, people like to first produce the materials, and then write the document. There is no reason why that should be different for reproducible reports.

I would like to make a web-based editor to write Rnw/Rmd. However, instead users iterating between updating their Rmd/Rnw files and running `knitr()`, I want a workflow as follows:
## Creating a new report
1. User creates a single R script that runs the study. No weaving.
2. When the script has been completed, user opens the script in the editor. The editor runs `evaluate()` once and stores the results-object. The results-object contains all code, console output, figures, etc that will end up in the report. The user is now done with R.
3. The user writes the report using standard markdown/latex or other document editing workflow. The obtained results (or previews) are displayed in a wysiwyg editor.
4. The editor creates the weaved code containing md/tex and original R code. The final result is a standard Rnw/Rmd script as we know it.
## Compiling / Editing an existing report
1. The user opens up the Rnw/Rmd file in the editor.
2. The editor runs the R code in the report once using `evaluate()`. Store all results.
3. as above.
4. as above.

To implement this, we need an alternative interface, that the decouples `knitr()` process the process in two steps:
1. The first function takes a .Rnw / Rmd document, runs `evaluate()` on the code and returns a list that contains both the R output (evaluate results-object) and latex/markdown code, in the original order. An R script is a special case of a Rnw document that contains no md/text, hence the output will identical to the output of `evaluate()`.
2. A second function compiles this list of R output an R output and md/tex into the final html/pdf/etc.

The `knitr()` function can then be implemented as simply running both these functions in sequence.

title: Plots overwritten with \input
description:
Hi - I'm using RStudio (0.98.1062) and knitr 1.7 to write a document large enough that I split it into different .Rnw files. I knit() each one separately and then use a "master" document with \input{} to compile the final PDF. I find that R plots in unlabeled chunks get overwritten. A tiny example is below. Create files called BasicPlot.Rnw and GGPlot.Rnw

BasicPlot.Rnw

```
\section{Basic Plot}
Make a basic plot
<<>>=
df <- data.frame(x=c(1,2,3,4), y=c(6,5,4,3))
with(df, plot(x,y, main="Basic Plot"))
@
More text goes here.
```

GGPlot.Rnw

```
\section{ggplot}
Make a ggplot
<<>>=
library(ggplot2)
df2 <- data.frame(x=c(1,2,3,4), y=c(16,17,18,19))
ggplot(df2, aes(x,y)) + geom_point() + labs(title="ggplot")
@
```

knit() them

```
knit("BasicPlot.Rnw")
knit("GGPlot.Rnw")
```

Make and compile to PDF this .Rnw

```
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
\input{BasicPlot}
\input{GGPlot}
\end{document}
```

The PDF contains either two of the plots from BasicPlot or two from GGPlot. Giving the chunks labels or putting the two R chunks in one .Rnw and not using \input fixes this. Is this a bug or newbie's ignorance?

Tex snippet: 

``` tex
<<begin>>=
#
read_chunk('extern-test.R')

## @knitr my-external-chunk

title: After knitr processed one chunk, it removed cache files of a previous chunk
description:
I can't reproduce the result with simple example. However, here is some information that might be helpful.

I have the following chunks, (I have to replace the "greater than", "less than" symbols to "||" otherwise the browser interface will eat the contents)

```
<<knitr_options, include=FALSE,cache=FALSE>>=
opts_chunk$set(fig.width=12, fig.height=4, fig.path='RnwFigs/',
               tidy=TRUE, cache.path="RnwCache/", cache = TRUE,
               echo = TRUE, results="markup", error=FALSE)
options(width=60)
@
[some extra blocks and code omitted]
<<FilterCases,dependson=c("CasesCandidateInfo","FilterForLowMAF"),engine="bash">>=
Code chunk 1...
@
<<mystop>>=
stop("Stop")
@
<<CasesInfo,dependson=c("BuildConfig","FilterCases"),engine="bash">>=
Code chunk 2...
@
```

As the first step, I ran knit, it stopped at chunk mystop. At this point, I looked at the RnwCache directory and saw the cache files,

```
[myname@computername RnwCache]$ ls -l FilterCases*
-rw-r--r-- 1 myname groupname 383 Oct 15 14:41 FilterCases_aba388ac21084852ae2d1583220af13b.RData
-rw-r--r-- 1 myname groupname   0 Oct 15 14:41 FilterCases_aba388ac21084852ae2d1583220af13b.rdb
-rw-r--r-- 1 myname groupname 113 Oct 15 14:41 FilterCases_aba388ac21084852ae2d1583220af13b.rdx
[myname@computername RnwCache]$ ls -l CasesInfo*
ls: cannot access CasesInfo*: No such file or directory
```

Then I moved the 3 lines of stop code to the end, and ran knit again, the result was:

```
[myname@computername RnwCache]$ ls -l FilterCases*
ls: cannot access FilterCases*: No such file or directory
[myname@computername RnwCache]$ ls -l CasesInfo*
-rw-r--r-- 1 myname computername 437 Oct 15 14:44 CasesInfo_733783b8c93875bfcfd8825b475e5350.RData

```

Since the cache files were lost, everytime I ran knit, it would re-run both chunks because the second depended on the first. This costed me time. title: parallel chunks
description:
I just made a [feature request at Rstudio](https://support.rstudio.com/hc/communities/public/questions/200958913-Spawn-multiple-knitr-processes-to-take-advantage-of-multicore-systems) and thought I'd lodge it here too.

I often use knitr to group my models with a bit of context etc. so I'll have something

``````
## Model1 
```{r}
slow_glmer_call
``` 
## Model2 
```{r} 
slow_glmer_call2
```
``````

I was wondering whether it would be feasible and/or interesting for others to add a order parameter to knitr chunks. Then, chunks which have the same order value could be automatically executed in parallel. 

For me, this would be nice, since I like having a nice readable reproducible report, but I also like not waiting hours for my 20 models to finish in sequence on one core out of eight.

I'm guessing the main barrier would be to do this automatically on different architectures, or does this also somehow go contrary to knitr's philosophy?

title: render_pandoc()

title: Chunk option to fully specify path to ImageMagick?
description:
In functions which make use of ImageMagick (e.g. `eng_tikz()`), it would me nice to have a chunk option to fully specify the path to the user's installation of ImageMagick (e.g. `windows_im_path = ""`). 

For Windows 7 users (and apparently Windows XP users as indicated [here](http://savage.net.au/ImageMagick/html/install-convert.html), Windows has another file named `convert.exe`. This file is located in the System32 and the steps outlined as an XP fix in the previous link do not work for me on two separate installations of Windows 7 - Windows appears to be giving System32 priority in the PATH variable regardless of its order in the PATH variable list. 

Continuing with the `eng_tikz()` example, I would implement something like the following logic in the definition of `eng_tikz()`: 

```
conv = ifelse(windows_im_path = ""
              ,system(sprintf('convert %s.pdf %s.%s', fig, fig, ext))
              ,system(sprintf('"%s" %s.pdf %s.%s', windows_im_path, fig, fig, ext))
)
```

This request is based on a rather hackish solution that I describe in a stack item located [here](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/26961773/imagemagick-path-not-being-recognized-with-engine-tikz-in-knitr).

title: Pass options to ImageMagick?
description:
In functions which make use of ImageMagick (e.g. `eng_tikz()`), it would me nice to have a chunk option to fully specify the path to the user's installation of ImageMagick (e.g. `im_opts= ""`). 

This may already be possible, but I can't seem to figure out how. 

Continuing with the `eng_tikz()` example, I would implement something like the following logic in the definition of `eng_tikz()`: 

```
conv =system(sprintf('convert %s %s.pdf %s.%s', im_opts, fig, fig, ext))
```

Thus, for example, if a user wanted to increase the density of png file created by ImageMagick, the user would specify `im_opts="-density 300"` and the options would then be passed in the system call to `convert.exe`. I haven't tested this solution (there may be some spacing problems with this approach), but the basic logic appears like it should work.

title: rmarkdown vignettes from R notebooks
description:
It would be nice to be able to create a vignette automatically from an R notebook (R scripts fed into `spin()`).  rmarkdown does this automatically when a `.R` file is passed to `rmarkdown::render()`.  This is actually very easy to do manually first calling `spin(knit=F)`, then moving the rmd file into the vignette folder.  However doing this automatically has a few issues.

My first attempt was to simply change the pattern at [utils-vignettes.R#L75](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/c77547ef3a5337fa85e2ac733969aaf5e1bbc69b/R/utils-vignettes.R#L75) to `[.][Rr](md|markdown)?$`.  This does not work however because `tools:::.get_vignette_metadata` expects the `%\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}` line to only contain leading whitespace, and the line in the `.R` file contains `#'  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}`, so the function return `#'knitr::rmarkdown` as the vignette engine, which is not a registered engine.

Changing the `tools::.get_vignette_metadata` function to remove anything prior to the metadata fixes that problem and you are able to successfully build the vignette with `tools::buildVignettes()`.

``` r
unlockBinding('.get_vignette_metadata', env=getNamespace('tools'))
assign('.get_vignette_metadata', function(lines, tag) {
  meta_RE <- paste(".*%+[[:space:]]*\\\\Vignette",
    tag, "\\{([^}]*)\\}", sep = "")
  meta <- grep(meta_RE, lines, value = TRUE, useBytes = TRUE)
  gsub(meta_RE, "\\1", meta)
}, getNamespace('tools'))
```

However this only works if you use `tools::buildVignettes(tangle = FALSE)`.  If you use `tangle = TRUE` the file gets overwritten by the tangled file.  I tried to remove the condition at [utils-vignettes.R#L46](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/c77547ef3a5337fa85e2ac733969aaf5e1bbc69b/R/utils-vignettes.R#L46) to disable tangle for the rmarkdown engine, but it did not seem to work.

It is very close to working, I just need a little guidance with the last few steps.

You can use [this gist](https://gist.github.com/jimhester/c9c659dbd0e8964b8829) as a test vignette if you get a chance.

I'm writing a vignette for rgl, using knitr and markdown to produce HTML output.  Using a variation on the hook_webgl hook function, I'm seeing inconsistent sizing of figures, depending on whether the vignette is produced by a recent Rstudio with pandoc, or an older one without pandoc.

I wrote a simple test vignette to illustrate.  It is available at http://www.stats.uwo.ca/faculty/murdoch/temp/knitrchange.Rmd.  It contains this hook definition:

hook_bug <- function (before, options, envir) {

    paste("dpi=",options$dpi,"fig.width=",options$fig.width, "fig.height=", options$fig.height)
   }

title: Literate programming for writing R packages
description:
Literate programming (LP) normally means _documentation_ for R packages, e.g. **roxygen2**. It is not really about programming (well, documentation is also part of programming). For data analysis / reporting, LP means Sweave/**knitr**, which is about programming, but it does not naturally apply to R packages. I mean the `R/` directory, not the `vignettes/` directory (the latter problem has been solved). Joe has an attempt in **shiny** ([reverted later](https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/pull/478)), which illustrates the demand that sometimes we do need to explain our code _beyond_ the documentation for end users, e.g. the implementation details that may not be so obvious when we read the source code and comments. The clever hack in **shiny** to achieve this goal was to create `src/Makefile` (even if there is no C/C++/Fortran code under `src/`), and run the Makefile to generate (tangle) R scripts into the `R/` directory dynamically. One very minor disadvantage is that this requires `make`. I guess there might be a pure R approach that can make this work without `src/Makefile`.

When the Rmd files have dependencies on each other, how do we determine the order to compile them? That is achieved by `@include` in **roxygen2**. Perhaps we can tangle the documents, build and install the R package, then come back and compile Rmd documents.

The Rmd documents look like this:

``````
This is for developers. Explain the gory details that users do not care.

```{r}
#' This is the title in Rd.
#' 
#' Description.
#' @param foo explanation
#' @param bar explanation
#' @export
f = function(foo, bar) {
  foo + bar
}
```

More gory details.
``````

We can even include example code that produces live output in Rmd (e.g. graphics), so we do not have to always read the hard, dead, and ice cold code under `R/`.

Or we can even parse the roxygen comments into Markdown and include them in the HTML output as well? (This may not be easy to achieve) Sounds like this may bring a whole new documentation system to R. I was dreaming about graphics output in Rd, but it never comes.

Just some random thoughts.

title: Embedding svg XML in output? (like self-contained w/o binary)?
description:
Hi @Yihui,

One frequent concern I have in my knitr files with respect to reproducible research is that I worry about overwriting an image linked in some knitr-generated output page, thus causing the figure displayed to be inconsistent with the code. (This is particularly easy to have happen when browsing older versions of the code, in which the image path is unchanged).  

Previously I've avoided this by pushing a new version of the image to an external site, like flickr, every time it is generated, such that no figure file is ever overwritten.  However, this is rather clumsy and not portable, since it requires my private flickr api keys (meanwhile options like imgur are not permanent, and any of these things feels like a hack). 

Your self-contained option is a rather more elegant way around this, keeping the output figure as part of the output document and thus avoiding the problem of changing the linked output.  However, as I can generate quite a lot of images and my output code is usually version managed in git, I'm hesitant to start committing a lot of `.md` and `.html` files full of binary encoding. 

I'd particularly like to use svg, both because the scalable vector graphics render much better on the web anyway, (particularly when supporting a variety of devices from smart phones to large monitors), and are plain text and thus version a bit more compactly. Unfortunately, this still raises the challenge of linking (made worse by the fact that we can embed pngs that are committed to github using raw urls but not svgs).  

It seems to me a good solution would be to have some kind of toggle that works rather like self-contained but spits out the XML content of the `<svg>` element rather than the binary encoding there of.  Perhaps this is something you would consider supporting as an option in knitr? (or point me towards how to do this with hooks if possible?)  

I'm not sure if from an interface perspective it would make sense to make this the automatic behavior whenever `self-contained=TRUE` and `dev='svg'` or if it should be it's own option, but I'm sure you have a good sense of that.  Anyway, thanks for your time and considering this!!

title: Support base64 image output
description:
Sometimes I need the Rmd to be not self-contained so that the HTML page does not include giant jQuery and Bootstrap libraries. But a side-effect is that image-producing chunks also result in standalone pictures in local directory.

Is it possible for knitr to support base64 image output so that the HTML is not self-contained for the JavaScript libraries but self-contained for the images (which is rendered and stored in HTML in base64 code)? In this case, I often want my images are included but the libraries are loaded from remote CDNs.

My current implementation of this looks like

``` r
library("htmltools")
library("caTools")
filename <- tempfile()
png(filename, width = 600, height = 400)
plot(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
invisible(dev.off())
bin <- readBin(filename, file.info(filename)$size, what = "raw")
file.remove(filename)
base64txt <- base64encode(bin)
tags$img(title = "plot of mtcars", src = paste0("data:image/png;base64,", base64txt))
```

Maybe an option for chunks can be added to indicate that this figure should be output as base64?

title: Couple small problems with setting fig.path and base.dir together
description:
I noticed two related problems when specifying a `base.dir` combined with specifying a `fig.path` that contains a directory (ie. has a path separator rather than simply being a filename prefix).

**1. An error comes up if the figure directory doesn't exist**  
This is the error I always get  

```
Error in png(..., res = dpi, units = "in") : unable to start png() device
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In png(..., res = dpi, units = "in") :
  unable to open file 'figdir/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png' for writing
2: In png(..., res = dpi, units = "in") : opening device failed
```

Steps to reproduce:   
- create a simple Rmd that generated a figure. I use this code in a file called `plotme.Rmd`
  
  ``````
  ``` {r}
  plot(runif(10))
  ```
  ``````
- set the `base.dir` to any directory that is not the current directory. For example, `knitr::opts_knit$set(base.dir = "outdir")`  
- create the `outdir` directory, otherwise knitr will error (not sure if this is a bug or expected?)  
- set the `fig.path` to a string that contains a path. For example `knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = "figdir/")`  
- knit the document.  `knitr::knit("plotme.Rmd")`  
- hopefully you also get the same error message as above  

**2. The `figdir` directory gets created in the wrong place and has nothing in it**  
When there is a `base.dir` defined and the `fig.path` contains a directory, then that directory is created both inside `base.dir` (which is correct), but it also gets created in the working directory.  
To reproduce, continue from the previous steps and just create a directory `figdir` under `outdir`.  Now running knitr works, but an empty `figdir` directory is created in the working dir.

---

Environment: Windows 7, R 3.1.2, knitr 1.8

title: Option to specify document output path?
description:
Hi Yihui,

We were grappling with this issue at #rrhack last week and would really love your input.  Currently we can specify output path only as a function argument (as far as I can tell anyway), e.g.:

``` r
knit("doc.Rmd", "papers/doc.md")
```

or with render:

``` r
render("doc.Rmd", output_file = "papers/doc.Rmd")
```

Ideally we'd be able to do: 

``` r
opts_knit$set(output.dir="papers")
```

and just hit the knit2pdf / knit2html button in RStudio instead.  Is that an option you would consider adding?  

The annoying part about this is that it is impossible to accomplish this same behavior with the `knit` button in RStudio, with the default assumption that the inputs (`.Rmd`) and outputs (`.md` or `.pdf` or whatever rmarkdown has been told to create) are in the same directory, which seems to be in direct conflict with much standard advice on reproducible research. Having to tell people to avoid the RStudio knit button and insist they type the command argument is clearly not ideal.  

Expecting input and output to be in the same directory is equally problematic though, for while it works well for small examples it really doesn't scale to projects that need some directory structure.  Your knitr book illustrates this issue nicely, where you write a script to call knit with explicit paths such that the `.Rmd` and `.md` end up in different directories. 

If this is interesting I'd be happy to send a PR, though you might implement it faster ensuring that it doesn't break anything. (There are also some finer points to consider: e.g. whether figure urls should or should not be made relative to the new `output.dir`; and whether `output.dir` is relative to `root.dir` or the source .Rmd dir, etc)

This might not completely solve the [working directory insanity](https://gist.github.com/jennybc/362f52446fe1ebc4c49f) but I think it would help. @jennybc and @hlapp might be able to put this better than I.

title: named logical always interpreted as TRUE when passed to eval
description:
Here is a MWE:

```
\documentclass[a4paper]{article}

\begin{document}

<<chunk1>>=
x <- 1
doChunk2 <- FALSE
names(doChunk2) <- "blah"
@

<<chunk2, eval = doChunk2>>=
x <- x + 3
@

<<chunk3>>=
x
@

\end{document}
```

When doChunk2 is named, it is interpreted as TRUE, so the final value of x is 4; when it is unnamed it is interpreted as FALSE, so the final value of x is 1. 

In my real application I did not name the logical value explicitly, the name was just kept from the object the logical value was computed from, causing this unexpected behaviour.

For example, in a common use case, I have one master document (e.g. `parent.rmd`) and several child documents, each with a number of chunks.

If I attempt to re-use the same child-chunks, however, this will fail:

**parent.rmd**

``` r
# settings
settings = list(...)

# run once
knit_child('useful_analysis.rmd')

# new settings
settings = list(...)

# run again
knit_child('useful_analysis.rmd')
```

To get around this, the two option are to either not use any chunk names for the child documents, which results in anonymous figure and cache names, or to use `knit_template()` in the parent document with `results=asis`:

cat(knit_child(text=unlist(knit_expand(file='useful_analysis.rmd'))))

title: Proposed function: knitr::custom_knit
description:
There's currently an undocumented ability to specify a `knit:` hook in Rmarkdown YAML headers and replace `rmarkdown::render` with something else in RStudio, as used for example in [slidify](https://github.com/ramnathv/slidify/commit/07794a3c2d228822c173c1ad5eacf5ab54a42062#diff-1), and which I describe further potential uses for in notes [here](https://github.com/lmmx/devnotes/wiki/Rmarkdown-custom-knit-hook-to-compile-a-multi-part-document).

This could provide a sort of `make` for Rmarkdown, with metadata-directed knitting of e.g. files that may be added through `includes:` in YAML headers, or as `{r child=...}` code chunk references within the document itself (see notes linked above for examples, and [this repository](https://github.com/lmmx/tomasetti-vogelstein-2015)).

Although a Knit button running the above is user-friendly, it's natural to want to be able to replicate the button's behaviour as a command, which I presume would be best placed in the `rmarkdown` package (thus available within RStudio by default).

@cboettig recommended in [this thread](https://github.com/ropensci/reproducibility-guide/pull/81#issuecomment-76936284) that there should be a way to call said custom function from the command-line.

I recommend a function e.g. `rmarkdown::custom_knit` :

``` r
custom_knit <- function(filename, encoding) {
    rmd.content <-  paste( readLines(filename) , sep = "\n" )
    yaml.range <- which('---' == rmd.content)[1:2]
    if (all(is.na(yaml.range))) { knit.function <- rmarkdown::render } else {
        yaml.header.range <- setdiff(do.call(seq, as.list(yaml.range)), yaml.range)
        rmd.yaml <- paste(rmd.content[yaml.header.range], collapse="\n")
        knit.hook <- yaml::yaml.load(rmd.yaml)$knit
        if (is.null(knit.hook)) {knit.function <- rmarkdown::render} else { 
            knit.func.str <- as.function(as.list(knit.hook))()
            knit.function <- eval(parse(text = call(knit.func.str)))
        }
    }
    return(knit.function(filename, encoding = encoding))
}
```

Running the function on for example the 'analysis.Rmd' file of [this example repo](https://github.com/lmmx/tomasetti-vogelstein-2015):

``` r
custom_knit('documents/analysis.Rmd', 'UTF-8')
```

would then run the same as the button in RStudio.
- The above handles both anonymous functions and those sourced as `package::function` (e.g. test with `knit: slidify::knit2slides` in YAML of `analysis.Rmd`). If no `knit:` hook is present it uses `rmarkdown::render` as the knit function.
- Do others feel it would be better suited to a modification of another function, e.g. as behaviour triggered by a parameter in some existing function? e.g.
  
  ``` r
  render(input, encoding, custom_knit = TRUE)
  ```

I [originally submitted](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/issues/389) this to the rmarkdown repository, but on second thoughts it seems more appropriate for knitr. If I've misunderstood please let me know and I'll reopen the other, thanks.

title: Which document is being knit?
description:
This is related to #564: My code needs to find out whether it’s being called from inside a knitr document. However, in addition to that, it needs to find out _which_ document is being knit, i.e. the full path to that document.

The background for this is klmr/modules#31: _modules_ needs to know the base path of its calling code in order to resolve relative import file locations. At the moment, it resolves to the directory of the code which kicks off the knitting process, which is usually not the correct directory.

Inside _modules_ I cannot fix this issue without requiring the user to manually specify the module base path, which I’d like to avoid.
## MWE:
- **`doc.rmd`**:
  
  ``````
  ```{r}
  devtools::install_github('klmr/modules')
  modules::import('./test')
  ```
  ``````
- **`test.r`**:
  
  ``` r
  message('I was called correctly.\n')
  ```
- **`script/knit`**:
  
  ``` r
  #!/usr/bin/env Rscript
  knitr::knit('doc.rmd', 'doc.md')
  ```

``` bash
chmod +x script/knit
./script/knit
```
### Expected output:

> […]  
> ## I was called correctly!
### Actual output:

> […]  
> ## Error in `modules::import("./test")`: Unable to load module `./test`; not found in `"./script"`

I'm willing to spend some time on this, and create a PR but just wanted to have your thoughts first.

title: Automatically derive fig.width from out.width
description:
Currently, when working with latex, I have to manually adjust the `fig.width` parameter in order to have my figure nicely scaled for the output size `out.width`. Consider e.g. the basic task of including a figure at full textwidth. To obtain a correctly scaled figure, I'd currently have to somehow obtain a numerical value for `textwidth` in inches (for me, this is something about 5.8in as I found out following [this answer on TeX.SE](http://tex.stackexchange.com/a/39385/64293)) and then set `fig.width` to this value. This is annoying, as 
a) I somehow have to look up the current value of `\textwidth`, 
b) this value can change depending on the document's parameters, and my code does not adjust,
c) I would consider it the most common use case that I want my figure to be scaled to the output size...

Is there a particular reason why this is not implemented? I was a little bit surprised how complicated this is. Did I miss something?

title: Support conditional formatting
description: Consider the following example: ``` rconsole > library(knitr) > df <- data.frame(name = c("James", "Ken", "Jenny"), age = c(18, 20, 22)) > kable(df) |name | age| |:-----|---:| |James | 18| |Ken | 20| |Jenny | 22| ``` Is there a recommended way to transform the output to a html table with conditional formatting like ``` |name | age| |:----|---:| |James|18| |Ken |20| |Jenny|22| ``` so that the background color of cells in column `age` gives a visual indicator of the magnitude of the cell value relative to other cells in the same column. One other possible use case is to make red texts in all `age` cells whose value >= 20 so that the produced code is ``` |name | age| |:----|---:| |James| 18| |Ken |20| |Jenny|22| ``` Basically, the feature may require that `kable` allow for some intermediate intervention by functions that transform the text to be put into the cell given its column name and its original value (e.g. numeric value).

title: Support svgz format to reduce file size
description:
HTML pages with some svg embedded are really large. Recently I notice that `svgz` is a gzip-compressed version of `svg` but I'm not sure if it is easy for knitr to support rendering plots to `svgz`. Maybe it should work in two passes: first, use existing svg renderers to produce svg, and output via gzip compression.

From the [a documentation](http://www.w3.org/TR/SVG/minimize.html) the huge html consisting of several svgs with many points should be largely reduced in file size.

I did some informal tests on this: 

Create a rmarkdown document with the following code chuck which generates 50 images.

``` r
library(PerformanceAnalytics)
invisible(lapply(1:50, function(i) {
  x <- xts(rnorm(500, 0.0001, 0.01), seq(as.Date("2010-01-01"), by = "day", length.out = 500))
  charts.PerformanceSummary(x)
}))
```

Here's some benchmark on my computer:

| HTML with | naked size | gzip size |
| --: | --: | --: |
| png | 4.1MB | 2.57MB |
| svg | 21.1MB | 2.35MB |

Really appreciate if anybody shows a way to correctly produce svgz.

The following posts may help:
1. http://graphicdesign.stackexchange.com.80bola.com/questions/24797/when-should-i-use-svg-or-svgz-for-my-web-graphics

title: `cache=1` or `cache=2` dont work with `cache.extra` technique
description:
I’m not sure if this is a bug or a design feature, but I thought I would mention it since it threw me off. As discussed in [Issue #238](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/238), using undefined chunk options to add additional requirements to the cache validation is very useful for checking for new input files. However, this does not work when `cache=1` or `cache=2`.

I think this is because `cache.extra` is not in the list of things that affect the cache for `cache=1` or `cache=2`:

``` r
# options that should affect cache when cache level = 1,2
cache1.opts = c('code', 'eval', 'cache', 'cache.path', 'message', 'warning', 'error')
# more options affecting cache level 2
cache2.opts = c('fig.keep', 'fig.path', 'fix.ext', 'dev', 'dpi', 'dev.args', 'fig.width', 'fig.height')
```

You can see this using the following chunk.  When `cache=1` or `cache=2`, it will pause the first knit, but not on following knits, whereas `cache=TRUE` always pauses.

`````` r
```{r cache=1, cache.extra=sample(1:1000)}
Sys.sleep(5)
``````

Should  `cache.extra`  be in `cache1.opts`? 

Thanks.

changes to code in chunk with child= option doesn't trigger cache changes
description:
I was testing how the caching worked when I imported another .Rmd file via `child=`. And I noticed that changes to code in the chunk that imported the child file didn't trigger changes to future chunks that depended on that chunk. 

Here's an example of the parent file

``````

---
title: "TestParent"
author: "Me"
date: "April 7, 2015"
output: html_document

---

```{r setupParent}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align="center", cache=TRUE, cache.path = "parent_cache/", message=FALSE, echo=FALSE, results="hide", fig.path="parent_figure/")
```

```{r bringInChild, child="test.Rmd"}
a<-5
b<-20
```
```{r anotherChunk}
u<-5
v<-20
```
Some text about Parent process. 

```{r useRun, dependson="bringInChild", chunk.comments=FALSE}
#note: if dependson refers to bringInChild, changes in that chunk (written in the parent file) don't trigger the chunk to rerun.
x2<-x*1000
y2<-y*1000
d<-14
Sys.sleep(10)
plot(x2,y2,main="Parent Plot")
```
``````

And here is the child file

``````

---
title: "Test1"
author: "Me"
date: "April 7, 2015"
output: html_document

---
```{r setup}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align="center", cache=TRUE, cache.path = "child_cache/", message=FALSE, echo=FALSE, results="hide", fig.path="child_figure/")
```

Some text about child process

```{r run1}
x<-seq(1,10,length=200)
y<-rnorm(n=200)
Sys.sleep(10) #so can easily see whether running caching
plot(x,y,main="Child Plot")
```
``````

If I change something in the child file, it triggers 'useRun' to recalculate in the parent file, which is good (and I can see because of the Sys.sleep(10) command in the 'useRun' chunk). You can also change 'useRun' to depend on 'anotherChunk' to see that if the child option is not set, changes do correctly trigger the caching (this is standard behavior and was to check that I was coding it correctly). 

But if I change `a<-10` in the 'bringInChild' chunk, it does not trigger the 'useRun' chunk to recalculate. If this is documented somewhere, i.e. that you shouldn't have code in this chunk, then it would be nice to have some kind of warning (sort of like if you do dependson for a chunk that is not cache=TRUE spits out a warning).

description:

A good approach would be to be able to run something like knit_parse() and get a list object with all the components of a knitr document - text chunks, code chunks, chunk options, and header metadata.

One use-case I was recently experimenting with is two-way conversion between Rmd and Jupyter Notebook files.

title: Add option to silently knit a child document
description:
Would it be possible to add an option to silently knit a child document? E.g. something like:

``````
```{r child='example.Rmd', silent=TRUE}
```
``````

It is already possible to hide all of the R code and results by setting `include=FALSE`, however Markdown/ `LaTeX` from the child document will still be included in the final output.

This could be very useful, for example, for generating two different types of output -- one that is verbose (including analysis text, code, etc.) and another that is more sparse and perhaps just includes a smaller number of figures and text that is in the parent document.

A work-around for now might be to create a `verbose` variable, and then move all of the Markdown, etc. into chunks that are only rendered when `verbose=TRUE`:

``````
```{r example_child_markdown, results='asis', eval=verbose}
 cat('Heading\n')
 cat('=======\n')
 cat('More text, markdown, etc...')
````
``````

However, while this is functional, it is not very elegant and reduces the overall simplicity and readability of the child documents.
