title: Cropping PDF fails with knitr > 1.10.5 under Windows.
description:
There seems to be a bug in knitr > 1.10.5 with cropping of PDFs under Windows.
Minimal example:

```
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
<<setup>>=
library(knitr)
knit_hooks$set(crop = hook_pdfcrop)
@

<<makeAPlot, crop = TRUE>>=
plot(1)
@
\end{document}
```

This works as expected (no warnings, plot is cropped) with knitr <= 1.10.5. 
It fails with knitr 1.11 and 1.11.2 (this is the version `install_github` installs, although according to the changelog there should be a version 1.12).
By "it fails" I mean that the PDF is not cropped and I get the following log (where I replaced German messages by a translation in []):

```
[Loading required package]: knitr


processing file: doc.Rnw
  |.............                                                    |  20%
  ordinary text without R code

  |..........................                                       |  40%
label: setup
  |.......................................                          |  60%
  ordinary text without R code

  |....................................................             |  80%
label: makeAPlot (with options) 
List of 1
 $ crop: logi TRUE

cropping figure/makeAPlot-1.pdf
pdfcrop.exe: Invalid argument.
pdfcrop.exe: Data: 4294967295
  |.................................................................| 100%
  ordinary text without R code


output file: doc.tex

Issues: 1 badbox

I suppose this is an unexpected side-effect of the recent changes in `hook_pdfcrop()` and `plot_crop()`.

title: Some non-ASCII characters disappear when knit()-ing
description:
When `knit()` a UTF-8 file (at least under Windows), some characters disappear under some circumstances. Here’s an example document:

```
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
æ, ø, å
1–2
\end{document}
```

Note that the charcater between 1 and 2 is an en-dash (U+2013). If I run `knit("knitrtest.Rnw", encoding="UTF-8")` on the file, the relevant part of the resulting `.tex` document contains:

```
\begin{document}
æ, ø, å
12
\end{document}
```

That is, the non-ASCII characters are correctly copied to the document (as UTF-8 byte sequences), but the en-dash disappears. (_All_ en-dashes in the documents seem to disappear.)

This is the bug. But a strange thing happens if I add, for example, a θ character:

```
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
æ, ø, å
1–2
θ
\end{document}
```

Running the same command, the en-dash appears, along with the θ character:

```
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
æ, ø, å
1–2
θ
\end{document}
```

So just adding a θ character somewhere in the document magically makes the bug disappear.

Things to note: This bug happens on Windows under Windows-1252 locale. The various characters have these properties (though all are stored as proper UTF-8 in the source file), which may perhaps be relevant(?):

\documentclass etc.: ASCII
æøå: non-ASCII, but available in ISO-8859-1 _and_ Windows-1252
–: non-ASCII, not available in ISO-8859-1 but available in Windows-1252
θ: non-ASCII, not available in either ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252, but available in Unicode

Also, when  I run the original file, which gives wrong output, no warnings are given. But if I run the file with a θ character, which gives the _correct_ output, the following warning is given:

```
Warning message:
In native_encode(text) :
  some characters may not work under the current locale
```

So if only `knitr()` would work like it does when an ‘exotic’ character like θ is included, everything would work fine!

title: chunk names must be unique between knitr documents in same directory
description:
This may be a user error/workflow problem rather than an issue with knitr itself, but I was just burned by this.

If you have multiple knitr documents (say Rmarkdown files) in a single directory _all chunks producing figures should have unique names between those documents_! My workflow consists of writing .Rmd documents, converting those to regular Markdown, and using [pandoc](http://johnmacfarlane.net/pandoc/) to produce a final PDF. From what I can tell, this is a pretty common workflow.

If .Rmd files produce figures with the same chunk name, then only the last figure produced remains in figure/. That means that all subsequent conversions from .md to .pdf reference only one version of a figure. This breaks the tie between the final document, and the code used to generate it.

It may be worth naming files in figure/ in such a way that they are explicitly tied to a report. Not sure what the cleanest solution would be: perhaps appending a short hash of the report file name to the .png file name. Alternatively, you could simple warn users that a file in figure/ already exists with that name and suggest they rename their chunk.

title: Can kable read format data from rmarkdown metadata?
description:
Hello, Yihui, do you think if it might be a useful feature for `kable` to obtain format info from `rmarkdown` metadata (https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/commit/61887a8cd9bd53258b3fd35c9df0f14f851e6ca3 )when the global option `knitr.table.format` is not available, at least for those common and official rmarkdown formats?

However, if we do get some formatted table outputs from `kable`, it will be easier for people to customize the results (like this [one](https://github.com/haozhu233/kableExtra) I'm currently working on).

``` r
#' Rmarkdown Format
#' @importFrom rmarkdown metadata
#' @export

rmd_format <- function(){
  rmd_output_metadata <- metadata$output
  rmd_fmt <- ifelse(
    is.null(rmd_output_metadata),
    "markdown", ifelse(
    rmd_output_metadata %in% c("html_document", "rmarkdown::html_vignette"),
    "html",ifelse(
      rmd_output_metadata %in% c("pdf_document", "rmarkdown::tufte_handout"),
      "latex", "pandoc"
    )))
  return(rmd_fmt)
}
```

title: automatically add appropriate cache.extra for source() etc commands in chunks
description:
I often `source()` quite computationally expensive scripts within an `*.Rnw`, and I a) would like therefore to have these results cached, and b) have it _automatically_ rebuild the cache if something changes in the `source()`ed script.

I imagine this is a relatively common scenario, and a "gotcha"-aspect of knitr caching: it's easy to forget that while a chunk is re-cached if its string content changes, it _will not be re-cached_ if some downstream, sourced script changes (makes sense, of course).

I've now solved this like so:

```
<<simulations, cache.extra = tools::md5sum("R/simulations.R")>>=
# this also caches again whenever the content of R/simulations.R has changed
source("R/simulations.R")
@
```

so, whenever I source a script, I also add a `cache.extra` to that effect.

Would it be feasible/desirable to add this kind of functionality as a default option, whenever a `source()` etc. are used?
Or does this just create more headaches for everyone?

title: Improvements to spin, making sense of working directories
description:
(Potentially related to #913)

Hi Yihui

As we discussed yesterday in the LA Shiny meetup, I have written a wrapper around `spin` that IMO makes it more usable for real-life scenarios.  I wanted to post it here to get your and other people's opinions.

[Vignette describing the problem and solution](https://github.com/daattali/rsalad/blob/master/inst/doc/spinMyR.md)  |  [Link to source code](https://github.com/daattali/rsalad/blob/master/R/spinMyR.R)

TL;DR of the vignette linked above: I use `spin` all the time and the main problem I have with it is that I have no way of using it with a complex directory structure. I like having my scripts in one directory, the inputs in another directory, and the output markdown/html in another.  `spin` assumes that the working directory is where the script lives, which is very often not the case, and `spin` doesn't let you control where the outputs go.  I made a function that wraps around `spin` in a way that I think is very easy to manage directories, and has a few other parameters too that I find useful.  I called it `spinMyR` because it was a block of code that I added to all my scripts that I would use to spin my R script.

If you agree that there is benefit in what I wrote, maybe it could be incorporated into knitr

Enjoy your visit home :)

title: run_chunk ?
description:
I suggest the addition of a `run_chunk` feature.  `run_chunk` would take loaded chunks (via `load_chunk`) and allow them to be run interactively.  This is particularly useful when sourcing a Rmd file for the purposes of debugging as Rstudio does not follow the empty chunk reference automatically.  It is also useful when there are dependencies between chunks and one doesn't want to always have to move around in the document to identify (and run) the relevant antecedent code.

An implementation might look something like:

```
#' Run a previously loaded chunk interactively
#'
#' Takes labeled code loaded with load_chunk and runs it in the /global/ envir (unless otherwise specified)
#'
#' @param chunkName The name of the chunk as a character string
#' @param envir The environment in which the chunk is to be evaluated
run_chunk <- function(chunkName,envir=.GlobalEnv) {
   chunkName <- unlist(lapply(as.list(substitute(.(chunkName)))[-1], as.character))
   eval(parse(text=knitr:::knit_code$get(chunkName)),envir=envir)
}
NULL
```

Per the contribution guidelines since this is a feature implementation I thought I'd make the suggestion here before doing any pushing and pulling.  Is this a feature you would consider adding to knitr?  Or does it already exist?

title: Should `spin` treat roxygen2 function documentation like R code?
description:
I thought it would be awesome to write an R package as a literate programming document, with the code itself producing part of the HTML documentation via `spin`. One issue I ran into while exploring this possibility is that roxygen2 documentation is treated as Rmarkdown by `spin`. I know that I can change the value of the `doc` option when using `spin` so that the roxygen2 comments are not parsed, but I would like my R files to compile with the default options so things like "compile R notebook" (ctrl + shft + K) work as expected. I also noticed I could comment out the roxygen2 documentation using `/*` and `*/`, but then it does not show up in the Rmd output.

In short, I would like to produce a document that can be spun using `spin`'s default options in which the roxygen2 function documentation is part of the code chunks. I can see a few ways this could be accomplished: 
- change the default value of the `doc` option. This is probably impractical since it would break a lot of people's code, but I think it is the most elegant solution. 
- allow `spin` option defaults to be read from a header in the "goat hair" R file. This would allow me to specify the `doc` option value in the R file itself. Maybe something like `##' doc = '^##\\s*'` at the start of the file. Another option could be added to specify the regex that corresponds to header lines (in this example `'^##'\\s*'`). I am willing to try to implement this addition if you are think it is useful. 
- Add a new type of commenting similar to `/*` and `*/`, except that R comments in between are displayed in chunks as R comments rather than being excluded like the `comment` option does. In my case I would wrap the roxygen2 function documentation with this type of syntax. 

I am just getting into using `spin` so I am sorry if I overlooked some existing functionality that can solve my problem. Thanks for everything!

title: Generating tikz graphics fails with chunk before preamble
description:
The following MWE runs without problems:

```
\documentclass{article}

<<knitr-setup, echo=FALSE, cache=FALSE, message=FALSE>>=
library(knitr)

opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  dev = "tikz"
)
@

\begin{document}
<<test>>=
plot(1)
@
\end{document}
```

As soon as the chunk `knitr-setup` is moved _before_ the preamble, compilation fails with the following error: `Error in getMetricsFromLatex(TeXMetrics)`.

The following code can be used to reproduce the issue:

```
<<knitr-setup, echo=FALSE, cache=FALSE, message=FALSE>>=
library(knitr)

opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  dev = "tikz"
)
@

\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}
<<test>>=
plot(1)
@
\end{document}
```

The problem seems to be that the knitr copies whole chunk `knitr-setup` to `test-1.tikz` which is invalid TEX code. Therefore I suppose this is a bug in knitr.

title: Wrapping warning messages in knitr is not consistent with R output
description:
There seems to be slight issue of inconsistency in how `knitr` wraps lines in warning messages (and error messages) compared to usual R output:

``` r
warning_fun <- function(){
  long_function_name <- function(){
    warning("this is a relatively long warning message which should be on new line.")
  }
  long_function_name()
}
```

On knitted PDF:

``` r
warning_fun()
## Warning in long_function_name(): this is a relatively long warning message
## which should be on new line.
```

On R console:

``` r
warning_fun()
# Warning message:
# In long_function_name() :
#   this is a relatively long warning message which should be on new line.
```

It seems that if I set `options(warn = 1)` then I get similar warning in R console (but warning itself is still on a new line):

``` r
options(warn = 1)
warning_fun()
# Warning in long_function_name() :
#   this is a relatively long warning message which should be on new line.
```

This seems minor issue itself, but I suspect this relates to the issue that some warnings and errors to become truncated in PDFs due to long function call:

``` r, error=TRUE
sqrt("aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa")
## Error in sqrt("aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"): non-numeric argu
```

On R console:

``` r
sqrt("aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa")
# Error in sqrt("aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa") : 
#   non-numeric argument to mathematical function
```

title: Animated plots, hook_ffmpeg_html and video format
description:
Since knitr 1.3, animated plots using `hook_ffmpeg_html` uses OGG video flies instead of MP4. I think it is a sensible default (although WebM would be equally good, according to [browser support](http://www.w3schools.com/html/html5_video.asp). However, would it be possible to have the file type as an option, so that people could, if needed, switch to MP4? 

It might be already possible, in which case I apologize: I couldn't find a way to do it. As far as I understand it, the file type is hard-coded in `hook_ffmpeg_html`:

```
mov.fname = str_c(sub(paste(fig.num, "$", sep = ""), "", 
    x[1]), ".ogg")
```

After a couple of trials, I couldn't find a way to do it manually. For instance, modifying directly `hook_ffmpeg_html` using:

```
knit_hooks$set(hook_ffmpeg_html = function(x, options) 
    ...
    mov.fname = str_c(sub(paste(fig.num, "$", sep = ""), "", 
        x[1]), ".mp4")
    ...
```

does nothing: output is still a OGG file. Or setting up a new `hook_ffmpeg_html_mp4`, which would be called by `opts_knit$get(animation.fun = hook_ffmpeg_html_mp4)`, results in an error. In the end, I'm not too sure what to modify or what option to change to make this choice possible.

By the way, I'm using knitr 1.5.
Mathieu.

title: Knitr PDF shifts a plot to the right
description:
A knitr PDF shifted a plot all the way to the right, outside of the page - I could see only the leftmost sliver of it.  I found what's causing it; looks like a bug:

I had some text before the code chunks.  The text began with #### , the markdown way to create a title (large bold font).  Then there was a chunk with some code, and immediately after it a separate chunk just calling the plot.  So, these #### (four # signs) two chinks above caused the plot to shift to the right.  What is interesting, ### (three # signs) do not cause any troubles.

Also, this shift happened only with knitr PDF.  Neither knitr HTML nor knitr Word had this problem. 

For what it's worth...

title: declare, extract, or remove 'rst2pdf' dependency
description:
CRAN wants me to declare an 'rst2pdf' SystemRequirement dependency on a couple packages with reStructured Text vignettes even though the vignetteBuilder 'knitr' is the package that actually requires it.  Since 'knitr' could feasibly remove this dependency in the future in favor of pandoc (or other rst-aware tools)  it doesn't make a lot of sense to make such a SystemRequirement declaration on my end since my packages are agnostic on which system tool 'knitr' uses to process the reStructuredText.

I see three possible solutions:

1) Extract the rst2pdf code into a new package which explicitly declares it as a SystemRequirement.  This could just be the rst vignette building code (which CRAN is now complaining about even though I've been using it for a couple of years) or could also include the 'rst2pdf' function which has the undeclared dependency.
2) Remove the dependency by instead handling reStructuredText vignette code using pandoc (whose SystemRequirement should be satisfied by knitr's suggested package rmarkdown).  Could directly make html vignettes or indirectly make pdf vignettes via latex.
3) Directly declare a SystemRequirement in 'knitr' on 'rst2pdf'.

I could help with whichever approach you'd think would be best.

title: Rendering Fenced Code Blocks as ~~~ when Rmarkdown -> Markdown
description:
I was wondering if there was a way for the rendering of rmarkdown to markdown files to produce fenced code blocks that use ~~~ instead of ````?

The reason I ask is because for some of my blog posts, I will write it in rmarkdown, convert it into markdown (using knitr) and then upload this to Github pages (in principle following the steps listed here - http://nicolewhite.github.io/2015/02/07/r-blogging-with-rmarkdown-knitr-jekyll.html). This was all fine when the markdown parser is set to redcarpet. 

Recently [Github Pages announced that starting on May 1st, 2016 it will only support kmarkdown as the markdown parser](https://github.com/blog/2100-github-pages-now-faster-and-simpler-with-jekyll-3-0). Switching to this parser results in all coding blocks no longer rendering due to the fact that kmarkdown doesn't support fenced coding blocks using ```:

I've been reading numerous posts online about kmarkdown's support for fenced coding blocks using ```:
- https://github.com/jekyll/jekyll/issues/2709
- https://github.com/jekyll/jekyll/issues/2711

It seems like it should work with a simple change to your `_config.yml`:

```
kmarkdown:
  input: GFM
```

This doesn't appear to work for me. But when changing the blocks to ~~~, it works fine. 

Thanks,

But as soon as I add this innocent piece of code, Knitr goes crazy and pandoc.exe explodes after spinning its wheels for an additional minute beyond what the file used to compile in. This error is displayed:
`pandoc.exe: out of memory
Error: pandoc document conversion failed with error 1`
I believe pandoc is stopping when it reaches about 2gb of memory. I used the developer commandline to set the limit up to 4gb. http://jonathanchang.org/coding/fixing-pandoc-out-of-memory-errors-on-windows and it made no difference. But if I comment out that one line, knitr works fine again.  
This included bit of R code is so inconsequential and prior to that one line being added knitr would finish compiling in about 5 seconds (and that is with a large data file loading).
I do show additional warning messages in the RStudio Markdown output window that displays as Knitr HTML is running on the Rmd file. But they do not seem to be relevant.  
When I can get to a Mac, I may try and run my Rmd file through Knitr HTML in RStudio there.

title: Parsing with multiple documentclasses
Extending knitr. Add package to preamble
description:
Hi,

First of all thanks for your work.

I am working on a package for data frame visualization [condformat](http://www.sergioller.com/2016-03-10-condformat-release.md). Summarizing, it allows to add conditional formatting rules to a data frame, and then it can convert the data frame to HTML or LaTeX.

The generated latex code relies on `\usepackage[table]{xcolor}`, and I would like to be able to add it to the preamble of the documents that use it. To give a simple example:
1. Install the package:
   
   ```
   devtools::install_github("zeehio/condformat")
   ```
2. Save this R-code on a `my_file.R`
   
   ```
   #'---
   #' title: "Titre"
   #' date: Fecha
   #' header-includes:
   #'  - \usepackage[table]{xcolor}
   #' output:
   #'  pdf_document:
   #'    keep_tex: TRUE
   #'---
   data(iris)
   library(condformat)
   mydataset <- iris[c(1:5,70:75, 120:125),]
   cosa <- condformat(mydataset) +
     rule_fill_discrete(Species) +
     rule_fill_discrete(Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length,
                        expression = Sepal.Width > Sepal.Length - 2.25,
                        colours = c("TRUE" = "#7D00FF")) +
     rule_fill_gradient2(Petal.Length)
   
   cosa
   ```
3. Open `my_file.R` and click on RStudio File/Compile Notebook.

As the `condformat` package maintainer, I would like to add  `\usepackage[table]{xcolor}` to the LaTeX preamble, however `knitr::set_header` does not seem to allow me to define my own packages (only `tikz`, `highlight` and few others are available).

Is there a way for me to add the LaTeX package in the preamble without writing the `header-includes` on each file? (Ideally `condformat` users would not need to know about LaTeX)

Thanks

title: Knit HTML - Recover from Error? {Feature Request}
description:
Hi,

Referring to the question on SO - http://stackoverflow.com/questions/36026131/knit-html-recover-from-error

Currently in case there is any error in the R code, Knitr aborts. Its a pain especially for large analysis jobs to lose 2-3 hours of output. Can we add a feature in Knitr that - 

Option 1 - Recovers the partially created HTML from tmp directories or anywhere else
Option 2 - Get Knit HTML to continue on errors and not halt the code.
Option 3 - Atleast save the already Knit HTML and then stop. 

Staying True to "faithful output" principle, because the code was wrong, the offending code and error must go to the Knitted HTML and then execution can either stop or continue depending on the programmer's preference.

Is there anyway that we can add this as a feature?

Thanks, Manish

title: Chunk option "size" does not work with "results = 'asis'" for LaTeX
description:
Hello,

If the chunk options "size" and "results" are used together,  e.g.

`<<sample1, echo=TRUE, size='footnotesize', results='asis'>>=`

the resulting LaTeX document lacks the `\footnotesize` following the `\begin{kframe}`, and I don't think that this is intentional.

Minimal example:

```
\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}

<<sample1, echo=TRUE, size='footnotesize', results='asis'>>=
X <- table(LETTERS[sample(1:10, 100, replace = TRUE)])

ltxtbl <- data.frame(
  Character = names(X),
  Frequency = as.integer(X),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, 
  check.names = FALSE
)

ltxtbl <- xtable::xtable(
  x = ltxtbl,
  align = c('l', 'p{0.6\\textwidth}', 'r'),
  caption = paste('This is a table.'),
  label = 'tab:table1'
)

xtable::print.xtable(
  ltxtbl,
  caption.placement="top",
  floating = TRUE
)
@

<<sample2, echo=TRUE, size='footnotesize'>>=
X <- table(LETTERS[sample(1:10, 100, replace = TRUE)])

ltxtbl <- data.frame(
  Character = names(X),
  Frequency = as.integer(X),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,

)

  label = 'tab:table1'
)

xtable::print.xtable(

  caption.placement="top",

)
@
\end{document}

description:

> Error in par(x) : parameter "j" in "mfg" is out of range
> Calls: <Anonymous> ... process_group.block -> call_block -> block_exec -> par2 -> par

minimal example below

``````
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(knitr)

```

This is a test of the global.par command

Change the `par` settings

y

This chunk causes an error based on the partition commands the global settings. The error is localised to this last chunk (the other chunks parse and render fine).

> Calls: <Anonymous> ... process_group.block -> call_block -> block_exec -> par2 -> par

If a `dev.off()` command is put in the second last chunk (the last chunk that uses a plot command with the partitioned setup), the error disappears and the last chunk works.

title: undefined highlight macro in python to (beamer) latex
description:
I was trying to use knitr in the latest RStudio to compile an `.Rnw` file with

```
<<engine='python'>>=
print("%s" % ("a"))
@
```

in it. This generates latex containing 

```
\hlipl{\%s}
```

which will not then compile because `\hlipl` is not defined in the latex headers.  This expression _is_ defined by the `highlight.sty` file that (latest version of) the python `highlight` package generates when it runs.  By default that file contains a line

```
\newcommand{\hlipl}[1]{\textcolor[rgb]{0.45,0.46,0.77}{#1}}
```

So a quick fix is to include that line in the header of the `.Rnw`. 

But it would be good not to have to do that.

title: dev.args have no effect if cairo_pdf is used as recording device
description:
If I set

```
options(device = function(file, width = 7, height = 7, ...) {
        cairo_pdf(tempfile(), width = width, height = height, ...)
    })
```

in the setup chunk, dev.args have no effect on any plots. As far as I understand, this is because dev.args are only passed to a couple of selected devices in `chunk_device`, however, according to the R manual for `dev.control`, things like background color (and presumably point size, as this is also not working for me) are part of what's copied. Therefore, the actual plot in `plot2dev` will have the default dev.args instead of user-specified ones.

title: With Rmd files, include=FALSE as chunk option breaks blockquote
description:
If a chunk located inside a blockquote uses `include=FALSE` as an option, a blank line (without the leading `>`) will be inserted, breaking the blockquote.

Rmd file example:

`````` Rmd
Test of `include = FALSE` in blockquotes

> ## This is a test
>
> ```{r, include=FALSE}
> set.seed(10101)
> x <- mean(rnorm(100))
> ```
>
> The mean is `r x`
>

There is an extra blank line that breaks the blockquote.
``````

md file generated by knitr:

``` md
Test of `include = FALSE` in blockquotes

> ## This is a test
>

>
> The mean is -0.090839
>

There is an extra blank line that breaks the blockquote.
```

title: include=FALSE and environments
description:
I've found that toggling `knit( ... , include=FALSE)` can do unexpected (to me) things to the environments that things are being evaluated in.  

To reproduce, do something like:
1. evaluate `knit( )` within a function
2. have a chunk in the document with `include=FALSE`
3. within that chunk `source()` a file that expects things already defined in the Rmarkdown file to exist.

This is with the CRAN version of knitr in R 3.3.1, on Debian sid.

Here's two variants on the problem.  First, here are the contents of three files:

`included.R`:

```
if (!exists("x")) { stop("included")}
```

and `not_included.R`:

```
if (!exists("x")) {  stop("not included")}
```

and `eval.Rmd`:

``````
```{r setup}
x <- 3
prerequisites <- c("x")
```
```{r included, include=TRUE}
source("included.R")
```
```{r not_included, include=FALSE}
source("not_included.R")
```
``````

Then to see the error, run e.g.

```
> Rscript -e "f <- function (x) knitr::knit(x); f('eval.Rmd')"
[ output truncated ]
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : not included
Calls: f ... eval -> eval -> source -> withVisible -> eval -> eval
```

Here's the other variant, that doesn't require `source()`ing:

If this is the file `eval2.Rmd`:

``````
```{r setup}
x <- 3
prerequisites <- c("x")
```

```{r included, include=TRUE}
if (!exists("x")) {
    stop("included, error without sapply")
}
if (!all(sapply(prerequisites,exists))) {
    stop("included, error with sapply")
} 
y <- x
```

```{r not_included, include=FALSE}
if (!exists("x")) {
    stop("not included, error without sapply")
}
if (!all(sapply(prerequisites,exists))) {
    stop("not included, error with sapply")
} 
y <- x
```
``````

then I get:

```
> Rscript -e "f <- function (x) knitr::knit(x); f('eval.Rmd')"
[truncated]
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : not included, error with sapply
Calls: f ... handle -> withCallingHandlers -> withVisible -> eval -> eval
```

Help!  I am confused.

title: cache.vars option not working properly
description:
The option `cache.vars` seems to only work properly when `envir = new.env()` is specified in the `knit()` call.

Example code: 

``````
# ```{r sample_chunk, cache=TRUE, cache.vars='test_cache'}
# test_cache <- rnorm(1)
# test_cache
# test_nocache <- rnorm(1)
# test_nocache
# ```
# 
# ```{r print}
# rm(list = ls())
# library(tools)
# lazyLoad(file_path_sans_ext(list.files(getwd(), recursive = TRUE, pattern = "sample_chunk"))[1])
# ls()
# ```
``````

If we don't specify `envir = new.env()`, `test_nocache` might be included in the cache. Indeed, if the object does not exists in the global environment when falling the function, it will be included. However strangely if `test_nocache` exists when calling `knit()`, it will not be included in the cache...
When using something like `knit("test.Rmd", envir = new.env())`, `test_nocache` will never be included.

I came to this problem when using RStudio. I have very large objects that I don't want to include in the cache, but store in .RDS files at specific locations. I'm then using code like `if (!exists(obj)) obj <- readRDS("obj.RDS")` in the following chunks. I want to cache all other objects in the chunk though. When using the RStudio button "Knit PDF", you can't specify the environment, and even if I use `cache.vars` it will try to save the file in cache.

title: global.par=TRUE forces all plots to be the same size
description:
Here's a minimal example:

```
\documentclass[a4paper,10pt]{article}
\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc}

<<setup, include=FALSE, cache=FALSE>>=
opts_chunk$set(results='markup', cache=TRUE, dev='cairo_pdf', fig.path='plots/', cache.path='cache/', fig.keep='high', fig.show='hold', fig.width=2, fig.height=2, tidy=FALSE, dev.args=list(pointsize=8))
opts_knit$set(global.par=TRUE)
@
\begin{document}
<<test1, fig.width=2.5, fig.height=2.5>>=
plot(1:10)
@
<<test2, fig.width=5, fig.height=5>>=
plot(1:10)
@
\end{document}
```

Basically what happens is that while graphics device of the second plot has the specified size, the plot itself has the same size as the first one. My guess is that this is because block_exec indiscriminantly saves all parameters, including pin, fin, and so on. Perhaps there should be a blacklist of parameters that are not cached.

title: knitr should interact better with `system` (R)
description:
As highlighted by [this question](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/27388964/rmarkdown-not-outputting-results-of-system-command-to-html-file), we sort of have to jump through hoops to get the output from a `system` call to print its output to HTML.

Consider the following simple .Rmd file:

``````

---
output: html_document

---

```{r test, echo = TRUE}
system("ls")
```
``````

The output of which is simply:

```
system("ls")
```

We can force the output to show up by hiding things from viewers:

``````

---
output: html_document

---

```{r test, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
system("ls")
```
```{r test_eval, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
cat(system("ls", intern = TRUE), collapse = "\n")
```
``````

Which produces the output one would expect from simply running the first chunk.

But this seems like a sub-optimal solution and I think runs antithetical to the spirit of `knitr`.

I'm not 100% sure this is a `knitr` problem (as opposed to an `rmarkdown` problem); please advise if so.

description:
There seem to be two problems with how knitr is rounding numerics in inline blocks:
1. Rounding to getOption("digits") decimal places, instead of significant digits
2. Limiting display to 15 significant digits, instead of the 22 generally supported in R

The below Rmd demonstrates both problems. I'm planning to submit a pull request with a proposed fix. 

---

``````
title: "knitr_rounding"
output: html_document:
keep_md: true

---

# Knitr uses decimal places instead of signficant digits

## Examples where inline value differs from R standard
```{r}
options(digits=1)
pi
```
knitr inline: `r pi`  
**pi to 1 significant digit should be 3, not 3.1**

```{r}
options(digits=2)
pi
```
knitr inline: `r pi`  
**pi to 2 significant digits should be 3.1, not 3.14**

## Technical details
To render numerics, knitr uses `round(x, digits=getOption("digits"))`. This is
problematic because `options("digits")` defines the number of significant digits
desired (see `?options` and `?print.default`). However, the digits parameter for
`round()` sets the number of decimal places, not significant digits. There is a
separate rounding function, `signif()`, which rounds to the number of signficant
digits. Also, the `format()` method by default converts a numeric to a string,
rounding to `getOption("digits")` significant digits.

# Knitr limited to 15 significant digits inline (R limit is 22)

## Example where inline value is differs from R standard
```{r}
options(digits=22)
pi
```
knitr inline: `r pi`  
**pi to 22 significant digits should be 3.141592653589793115998**

## Technical details
knitr uses `as.character()` and `sprintf()` to convert numerics to strings.
However, `as.character()` only supports up to 15 significant digits (see
`?as.character`), while R generally supports 22 significant digits. The
`format()` method is an alternative that supports the full 22 digits, and also
provides rounding for numerics.
``````

title: Extending knitr chunk options
description:
@hafen and I have a goal to lazy-load html widgets when producing a html_document with rmarkdown.

We have successfully done that here: https://github.com/hafen/lazyrmd/blob/master/R/knit_print.R . This is accomplished with the chunk parameter `lazy = TRUE` and producing a `htmlwidget` object in that chunk.  (The htmlwidget is then produced in a stand alone page.  This dramatically reduces the initial load time (30+ seconds to a couple seconds) for the website when there are multiple (10+) htmlwidgets.)

I am wondering where I should submit a PR to have this option adopted/extended.  If knitr has a method to extend chunk options, I'd be happy to make sure htmlwidgets does this. If not, I'd be happy to submit this to knitr as a new chunk option.

Thank you for your time!

Best,
Barret

title: How to control space between text ,code chunk and the output
kable(caption = ...) bug:  no label set in latex output.
description:
If you do something like

```
<<ident>>=
kable(diag(3), caption = "The identity matrix")
@
```

in a `knitr` document targeting LaTeX output, it looks as though the intention is that you should be able to reference that table using `\ref{tab:ident}`.  However, this is done using a function `create_label` in the `R/utils.R` file, and that function has an argument `latex = FALSE`.  In order to get the label set, it needs to be called with `latex = TRUE`.  `kable()` doesn't do this. 

I think the fix is to change

```
# create a label for bookdown if applicable
if (!is.null(caption) && !is.na(caption)) caption = paste0(
  create_label('tab:', opts_current$get('label')), caption
)
```

to

```
# create a label for bookdown if applicable
if (!is.null(caption) && !is.na(caption)) caption = paste0(
  create_label('tab:', opts_current$get('label')), caption, latex = format == 'latex'
)
```

title: Option `size="normalsize"` doesn't mean LaTeX's normalsize
description:
I'm not really sure if this is an issue, but option `size="normalsize"` doesn't mean that the output is in LaTeX's normalsize, but that the current size from the document is used. (See https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/74670a18d/R/hooks-latex.R#L173)

So if the text in the document differs from normalsize, this may not be the user's expected result:

```
\huge
<<size="normalsize">>=
cat("Test")
```

title: a plain knit vignette engine?
description:
Hello.  I've created a 'plain' vignette engine which only calls knit, and leaves the rest of the creation of .html's and .pdf's to the Makefile.  A few things (beamer slides, biblatex+biber) are tidier in a Makefile than they would be compiling within R.  Would this warrant inclusion in the knitr package?

```
tools::vignetteEngine(
        'plainKnit', 
        weave=  function(file, ...) {
            # create a dummy .tex file so R CMD doesn't complain
            # make will discover that the .md file is newer and overwrite
            texFile = gsub("\\.[Rr](md|nw)$", ".tex", file)
            file.create(texFile)
            knitr::knit(input=file, ...)
        },
        tangle = knitr::purl, 
        pattern = '\\.[Rr](md|nw)$',
        aspell = list(
                filter = knitr::knit_filter
        )
    )
```

the Makefile:

```
all: slides.pdf document.html

clean:
    rm -rf *.tex *.toc *.bbl *.blg *.aux *.out *.log *.spl *tikzDictionary *.md figure/ cache/ *.dvi *.4* *.css *.idv *.lg *.tmp *.xref *.gz my*.bib *.nav *.xml *.vrb *.snm 

%.md: %.Rmd
    R -e "knitr::knit('$<', '$@', encoding='UTF-8')" 

%.tex: %.md
    pandoc --standalone --smart --to=beamer --output=$@ $<

%.bcf: %.tex
    xelatex $<

%.bbl: %.bcf
    biber $<    

%.pdf: %.tex %.bbl
    xelatex -interaction=nonstopmode $<;
    xelatex -interaction=nonstopmode $<

%.html: %.md
    pandoc --standalone --filter=pandoc-citeproc --self-contained --output=$@ $<
```

title: Tables inside of fullwidth environment with tufte book fail to render or render ugly
description:
The tufte book latex class (and many derived classes) have a `fullwidth` environment.  If the table function is `pander`, the latex typesetting engine will fail to parse the file.  If its `kable`, the table will print as unformatted text, as though `kable` wasn't aware that it was supposed to produce latex, unless it is given the `format="latex"` parameter.  If the parameter is given, `kable` will produce the table, but without proper formatting - it will have grid lines for every row and column all of the same weight instead of the nice pretty tables `kable` usually produces. 

I'm not sure to what extent this is a `knitr` issue vs. a `pander` issue vs. a `tufte-book` issue.

However, specifying engine =='asis' works (no error and only echos asis chunks).

title: Embedding knitr  generated tex files into a bigger latex.
description:
Hello.
I've already asked at https://tex.stackexchange.com/questions/342360/embedding-knitr-tex-files-on-a-bigger-latex-file but I'm getting no answers.

There are already some question about about how to use Knitr's latex output within a new knitr document, using Rstudio and include or input and declaring some chunks as child.

But what if I want to use a simple knitr output (such as an R xtable) from within an external LaTeX program, such as TeXStudio to build a larger project?

For example, I could create a mytable.rnw file and generate this simple table,

```
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}

<<r table2, results='asis', message=T, echo=F>>=

library(xtable) 
print(
  xtable(
    head(iris),
    caption = 'Iris data'
  ),
  comment = FALSE,
  type = 'latex'
)

@

\end{document}
```

![](https://i.stack.imgur.com/eFzF0.png)

And now I want to grab the generated mytable.tex file and use it in a bigger document from TexStudio, in the same folder.

```
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
 First table:
 \include{mytable}
 Second table:
 \include{mytable}
\end{document}
```

When I try to compile it I get many errors:

```
Can be used only in preamble. \documentclass
Can be used only in preamble. \documentclass{article}\usepackage
```

I guess the problem arises because knitr ouput includes a lot of preamble information that can't be included within the document body, not only usepackage directives but also a lot of fie-tune information about colors, tables...

What's the proper way do it? How to force Rstudio's knitr to output only the proper information?
Or how to force my main latex document (from TexStudio) to correct the problem?

If we have to do it many times is there any easy way to include that preamble in the main tex document without going manually one by one.
Or even worse, some genetared outputs may contain incompatible preambles.

@

In Rstudio, I source the Rnw (this step is important). If a figure exists in the Rstudio UI, I run the following:

library(knitr)

buff = tools::texi2pdf(file = outTexFile, clean = T)
```

The pdf produced is blank.

When I use the following Rnw (notice the # at the end of the chunk):

```
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
\begin{center}
<<echo=FALSE, out.width='1\\linewidth', fig.width=15, fig.height=17, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE >>=

if(T){

```
Then the figure appears in the pdf.

title: request for built-in python3 engine
description:
It takes a very tiny tweak to the existing "generic" engine (the one used for 16/25 of the engines, as indicated by

```
table(sapply(knit_engines$get(),function(x) isTRUE(all.equal(x,knit_engines$get("python")))))
```

to allow the use of python3 instead of python.  All I had to do was add a `python3` tag in 

```
else paste(switch(engine, bash = "-c", coffee = "-e", groovy = "-e", 
        node = "-e", perl = "-e", python = "-c", python3 = "-c", ruby = "-e", 
        scala = "-e", sh = "-c", zsh = "-c", NULL), shQuote(paste(options$code, 
        collapse = "\n")))
```

That seems like a fairly harmless/incremental change (although I guess ultimately if the list expanded too much it might make more sense to build this as a named list that associated command-line switches with engines).

This is easy enough to work around with my own custom code, but it would be nice to add it to the package.  

Could submit a pull request if that's your preference.

title: Filter / remove certain outputs after calling 'evaluate'?
description:
See associated discussion in https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/pull/979 -- non-printing data.table expressions still return a `NULL` output, and those outputs cause breaks in the otherwise contiguous source code.

My initial thought on a potential fix: the `evaluate` hook returns a list of sources and outputs, for which some of those outputs are `NULL`. From a debugger set on the `evaluate` hook:

```
Browse[1]> str(result)
List of 9
 $ :List of 1
  ..$ src: chr "suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))\n"
  ..- attr(*, "class")= chr "source"
 $ :List of 1
  ..$ src: chr "dt <- data.table(x = 1:5, y = 6:10)\n"
  ..- attr(*, "class")= chr "source"
 $ :List of 1
  ..$ src: chr "\n"
  ..- attr(*, "class")= chr "source"
 $ :List of 1
  ..$ src: chr "dt[, z := 1]\n"
  ..- attr(*, "class")= chr "source"
 $ : NULL
 $ :List of 1
  ..$ src: chr "dt[, k := 2]\n"
  ..- attr(*, "class")= chr "source"
 $ : NULL
 $ :List of 1
  ..$ src: chr "dt[, l := 3]"
  ..- attr(*, "class")= chr "source"
 $ : NULL
```

Would it be possible / appropriate for `knitr` to explicitly filter certain kinds of outputs? Currently, `NULL` outputs cause a line break to be inserted between otherwise bundled lines of code. I wonder if:

1. `knitr` should remove `NULL` outputs? (This might be too aggressive); or
2. `knitr` could remove outputs with some custom class, e.g. `empty_output`.

title: Malformed XHTML
description:
Knitr produces a tag at the top that states it is generating XHTML. If the MIME type is reported properly to the browser then the Knitr generated file will not render (one can simulate this easily by changing the extension to xhtml of the generated file). XHTML parsing is strict in browsers, I would recommend that Knitr produce an HTML tag which will allows for errors and most browsers will properly render even when there are errors.

I think the underlying cause is that javascript is not escaped properly via the XHTML standard. We have automated processes generating documents, which are then picked up *correctly* as XHTML for browser viewing--that are then non-renderable.

description:
Markdown child documents were added in #268 but the [documentation of `knit_child`](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/ccc2365661b4a0e994ffe1b291b657865b94902e/R/output.R#L379) refers to  https://yihui.name/knitr/demo/child/ which describes Latex child documents only. Would it be possible to include Markdown child documents  in the package documentation or on the yihui.name site?

An example of markdown child document was provided [here](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/inst/examples/child/knitr-main.Rmd), so it's probably just a matter of including this example in the documentation. I would have liked to comment on https://yihui.name/knitr/demo/child/ , but comments are closed on that page. 

Markdown child documents is a relevant topic and there are people [asking about it on Stackoverflow](http://stackoverflow.com/search?q=markdown+child+document).

title: Modify the or add a new vignette engine to build rst vignettes with pandoc instead of rst2pdf?
description:
If desired I can probably write a patch but I'd like to know your implementation preferences (see below), CRAN/hadley has had issues with getting rst2pdf on some of their testing machines and I wonder if they are widely supporting pandoc now (are they?) then perhaps this would be more convenient all around.

1) Should this be done as the default rst vignette engine instead of rst2pdf and hence should I add a new rst2pdf engine for those who want it or keep the existing behavior and add this as a new engine?   Although the former would break reverse compatibility it might be the better default for CRAN and I'm not sure how many people besides me would be affected and I don't care as long as a nice document is produced in the end.

2) Would it be better to use knitr's pandoc utility conversion function or rmarkdown's pandoc utility conversion function to do the rst to html or pdf conversion?  Doing the latter would make the package author's need to suggest rmarkdown for a non-markdown vignette but would reinforce the pandoc dependency.

3) Would it make sense to generalize the knit2html function to handle non markdown files or easier to add a new function just for rst files that would be called when it detects an rst file (like it does now)?

title: Issue with kable and ( in the first col.names
description:
There is an issue with kable when the first col.names entry start with a "(" and there is no row.names. E.g.:

Works:

```{r}
x <- matrix(1:10, nrow = 5, ncol = 2,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("x1", "x2")))

knitr::kable(x)
```

Does not work

```{r}
x <- matrix(1:10, nrow = 5, ncol = 2,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("(x,y]", "something")))

knitr::kable(x)
```

A quick workaround is:

```{r}
x <- matrix(1:10, nrow = 5, ncol = 2,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("\\relax(x,y]", "something")))

knitr::kable(x)
```

title: Using .Rbuildignore
description:
It seems knitr is ignoring the .Rbuildignore file when deciding what .Rmd files to knit. 

roxygen2 was recently edited to allow it to ignore what is in .Rbuildignore so you can see example code [here](https://github.com/klutometis/roxygen/blob/master/R/utils.R#L106)

Reproducible example: add the name of a knitr .Rmd file to your .Rbuildignore.
Expected result: the .pdf does not end up in the .tar.gz of the package.
Actual result: the .pdf does end up in the .tar.gz file. Also `R CMD check` gives a WARNING.

title: asis_output overrides header-includes in .Rmd file
description:
In a .Rmd file, if you include a list of `rmarkdown::latex_dependency` objects in the `meta` argument to `asis_output`, this will override any `\usepackage` statements in the `header-includes` argument. See the attached mwe. This came up in hughjonesd/huxtable#7.

[knitr-bug-mwe.Rmd.zip](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/files/965951/knitr-bug-mwe.Rmd.zip)

A workaround is to use the `includes` argument to `pdf_document`.

title: using expression(italic(...)) produces pixelated text in plots with cairo_pdf in R 3.4
description:
minimal example:
```
\documentclass[a4paper,8pt,notitlepage]{extreport}


<<setup, include=FALSE, cache=FALSE>>=
opts_chunk$set(dev='cairo_pdf', fig.path='plots/', cache.path='cache/', fig.keep='high', fig.show='hold')
@

\begin{document}

<<test, cache=FALSE>>=
plot(1:10, ylab=expression(italic(test)))
@

\end{document}
```
Note that ylab appears very pixelated. This only happens within knitr, when running
```
cairo_pdf('test.pdf')
plot(1:10, ylab=expression(italic(test)))
dev.off()
```
from the R console, everything is fine. Also recording and replaying a plot from the R console looks fine. This is specific to cairo_pdf, the standard pdf device works fine. Unfortunately, I have to use cairo_pdf.

title: Package does not build on read-only FS
description:
I am trying a bazel based build system for R packages, and knitr package build fails on this system because it tries to overwrite one of the input files. The input files are mounted as read-only in this build system, and I can not make an exception for knitr.

The problem code is here:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/14ee27c0ac448559e1c4cc3916f50ccd7f247336/R/citation.R#L109

This code tries to read the file `inst/misc/tweak_bib.csv` on package load, reorder it, and then write it back as the original file. This is non-standard behavior and as far as I can see, does not lead to any functional difference. The list to manually tweak is read from the csv, reordered, and cached in the package's namespace. The file `inst/misc/tweak_bib.csv` is never read again anywhere else. I can understand that writing it back would have helped in debugging when originally writing that function.

Can you please please consider removing that line? I am able to build 100+ R packages using my build system but knitr is the only exception because of this behavior.

I will appreciate any help you can provide.

Thanks.

title: Nested child documents require full path
description:
When I have nested child documents it seems that the directory is changed so I have to use the full path.

This seems a bug to me, but I might be wrong.

For example, I have a project made of master.Rmd, child.Rmd, childchild.Rmd, all in the same directory.

In `master.Rmd` I place the YAML to process my R-markdown document as html and include the file child.Rmd, for example:

     ---
     title: "Untitled"
     output: html_document
     ---

     ```{r child='child.Rmd'}
     ```

In `child.Rmd` I have

      sometext
   
      ```{r child='childchild.Rmd'}
      ```

When I try to compile `master.Rmd` to html, it fails complaining that it can't find `childchild.Rmd`.

If I change the content of `child.Rmd` to

      sometext
   
      ```{r child='/full/path/childchild.Rmd'}
      ```
Then everything works flawlessly.

I am not sure if it is a bug, but I think it would make sense that the full path is resolved from `master.Rmd` and applied to all children, which is best when authoring a multi-author document where the paths could differ.

Regardless of the decision on how to tackle this, thanks for reading Yihui!

title: Leiningen engine cannot not execute clojure code with dependencies
description:
Currently the leiningen engine can only evaluate clojure code which does not use any external clojure library.
This makes it in practice impossible to use clojure in knitr documents.

```{r engine="lein"}
(use '[clojure.core.matrix :as m])
```
fails with:

```
clojure.lang.Compiler$CompilerException:  Caused by: java.io.FileNotFoundException: Could not locate clojure/core/matrix__init.class or clojure/core/matrix.clj on classpath"
```

The "lein exec" plugin used by the lein engine does allow to use the dependencies of a leiningen project file in the same folder, if present.
This just requires to call "lein exec -ep" instead of "lein exec -e".

To change this would be fully backwards compatible, as a missing "project.clj" file is simply ignored, and so in this case "-ep" it has the same behavior as "-e".

title: knitr creates a copy of evaluate::evaluate as the default evaluate hook value
description:
The default `evaluate` hook is defined as:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/0d648a67275cda5f554a0d724dc2bb4ab0c7dd6f/R/hooks.R#L9-L14

This means that the default hook is tied to whatever version of `evaluate` was available at the time `knitr` was installed. If the version of `evaluate` changes, the knitr hook is not changed to reflect the new definition of `evaluate::evaluate`.

This explains errors like:
```
Quitting from lines 9-10 (helloworld1.Rmd)
Error in evaluate_call(expr, parsed$src[[i]], envir = envir, enclos = enclos,  :
  unused argument (include_timing = include_timing)
Calls: <Anonymous> ... call_block -> block_exec -> in_dir -> evaluate -> evaluate_call
```

Reported here:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/40198189/r-markdown-error-in-evaluate-call-when-knitting-any-rmd-file

We have also seen this problem when trying to use knitr inside a packrat cache. In the packrat scenario, we may be using the same version of knitr with multiple versions of evaluate (depending on a particular piece of content).

You probably can avoid this issue with something like:
```r
.default.hooks = list(
  # ...
  evaluate = function(...) evaluate::evaluate(...)
  # ...
)
```

title: export 'wrap' for use by other packages defining custom engines?
description:
Motivation: I'm working on defining a custom Python engine using the `reticulate` package, and I'd like to be able to interleave input and output in a similar way as to what we get when running R code chunks. This implies mimicing the output format produced by `evaluate::evaluate()`, if I understand correctly.

These outputs are generally post-processed using the `knitr` `wrap()` function. Would it be sensible for `knitr` to export this function? Or is there another API that I should be considering here? (Note that `engine_output()` seems to assume that a single block of source code is followed by a single block of output; I'd like to do something a bit more nuanced if possible)

title: 100% brew
allow users to override how inline chunks are executed?
description:
This is somewhat in line with the `evaluate` hook -- would it be possible for `knitr` to allow for users to control how inline chunks are evaluated as well? Perhaps with a hook like `knit_hooks$get("evaluate.inline")`?

This is mainly to support two kinds of features:

- Notebook execution of inline code chunks (not currently implemented, but something we might want to do in the future);

- Packrat-style dependency parsing (wherein we override the `evaluate` hook to instead discover dependencies).

(I guess, in principal, the same concern applies to PDFs, though file size is usually less of a concern there).

title: R chunk inside blockquotes has extra >
description:
For different reasons users want to use R chunk inside blockquotes. With knitr 1.17, when users try to do it the Markdown blockquotes has some extra `>`, used as the [markup for blockquotes](https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/syntax#blockquote).

# Minimal Reproducible Example

````
---
title: Foo
output:
  md_document:
    variant: markdown
---

```{r, eval = FALSE}
x <- 2

x <- x + 1
```

> Foo bar ...
>
> ```{r, eval = FALSE}
> x <- 2
>
> x <- x + 1
>
> x <- x + 1
> ```
````

# Expected behaviour

````
---
output:
  md_document:
    variant: markdown
title: Foo
---

``` {.r}
x <- 2

x <- x + 1
```

> Foo bar ...
>
> ``` {.r}
> x <- 2
>
> x <- x + 1
>
> x <- x + 1
> ```
````

# Knitr 1.17 behaviour

````
---
output:
  md_document:
    variant: markdown
title: Foo
---

``` {.r}
x <- 2

x <- x + 1
```

> Foo bar ...
>
> ``` {.r}
> x <- 2
> >
> x <- x + 1
> >
> x <- x + 1
> ```
````

# Acknowledges

This was first reported by @mfoos at https://github.com/swcarpentry/r-novice-gapminder/issues/314#issuecomment-337096826.

I currently use the `base::interactive()` to see if I should output to the viewer or to the stdout in case the document is being knitted for my `htmlTable:::print.htmlTable`. This works great in RStudio but I noticed that with `devtools::build_vignettes` the tables in the vignette are outputted to the viewer instead of into the document. I have currently solved this by using `options(interactive = FALSE)` but it seems clumsy and I wonder if you would consider either:
1. Redirecting stdin during knitting (not sure this is possible)
2. Providing a `knitr::is_interactive` function that I could rely on to check if the document is being knitted.

title: render multiple resolutions for bitmap engines
description:
It appears to me that upstream uses of `knitr`, especially when they are outputting to HTML such as `bookdown` ([this issue](https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown/issues/316)) and `blogdown`([this issue](https://github.com/rstudio/blogdown/issues/46) might require *several* resolution versions of bitmap assets, for example to support responsive images (say, download a different filesize depending on the viewport).

I think this is not presently possible, hope I am not wrong.
Unfortunately, I am a little bit confused of how or where (in `knitr`?) this could be implemented, but I hope it's at least a worthwhile thought.

Perhaps, `knitr` could learn to accept a *vector* of resolutions for `dpi`, and then upstream functions such as `blogdown` or `bookdown` could supply reasonable default sets of DPIs, to which `knitr` could render?

Ps.: There is also a more limited use case for this when non-R raster images are included via `include_graphics()`. When the bitmap is large, we might want quite *different* resolutions for a PDF output, and an HTML output, where load times matter more. This would require re-sizing in R as per [this issue](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/1273), and is probably a really *niche* use case.

title: Please consider changing the default setting for auto_pdf to 'FALSE'
description:
Hi Yihui, 

The auto_pdf parameter in include_graphics is by default 'TRUE'. To deactivate it, we must remember to type something like:

    knitr::include_graphics("myfile.png", auto_pdf = FALSE)

I appreciate the motivation for auto_pdf=TRUE, and have read ?knitr::include_graphics . However, last month, working to a deadline with multiple files, I ended up distributing to **hundreds of people** a file which contained within it an inappropriate .pdf instead of the correct .png file. That R ignored the filename I gave it and selected a different file (same name, different extension) led to an embarrassing result.

IMO it's too much of a liability to use TRUE as the default setting for auto_pdf. To my mind, the high cost to a few unlucky users such as me should outweigh the incremental aesthetic benefits gained elsewhere.

I hope I've explained adequately the problem lurking in auto_pdf's current default, particularly for novice users - Kevin from support.rstudio.com thought it might be worth bringing up with you, hence this post. Thanks for listening.

title: Unknown bug arises from using cache = TRUE & data.table
description:
I'm going crazy from this; apologies in advance for not being able to provide a reproducible example -- my data set is quite large (hence the need for `cache`).

I have the following code in a chunk:

```
DT[DT[ , .(w = sum(V1)),
              by = .(id1, id2)
              ][ , .(m = median(w)), by = id1
                 ][ , .(id1, h =
                          cut(m, breaks = break_vals,
                              include.lowest = TRUE, right = FALSE))],
      .(id1, id3, h, V1), on = .(id1)
      # there are about 1,000,000 rows in the result here
      ][ , median(V1), by = h]
```

When I run it from a fresh session, there's no problem. And when I load the data into memory, it runs fine, as well.

However, when the chunk used to create `DT` is created with `cache = TRUE`, this chunk errors:

> Error in `gmedian(week_hrs)` : negative length vectors are not allowed
Calls: <Anonymous> ... eval -> eval -> [ -> [.data.table -> gforce -> gmedian

`gmedian` is an internal `data.table` function. That `[.data.table` got dispatched suggests it's not the kind of problem that arises with `data.table` being loaded from binary where we need to `setDT` the object if it's added with, e.g., `load`. In fact if I add everything before the last `median` call in a chunk just before this one it runs completely fine:

```
cat(capture.output({
  DT[ , .(w = sum(V1)),
                by = .(id1, id2)
                ][ , .(m = median(w)), by = id1
                   ][ , .(id1, h =
                            cut(m, breaks = break_vals,
                                include.lowest = TRUE, right = FALSE))],
        .(id1, id3, h, V1), on = .(id1)]
}, sep = '\n')
# to prevent it running the erroneous chunk
stop()
```

Which assures that `DT` is still being treated as a `data.table`, that `GForce` is being dispatched correctly (the `m = median(w)` line dispatches `GForce`), up through that point.

Further, if I replace the real `V1` with `V1 = rnorm(.N)` to try and generate anonymized data to share here, the code does not reliably error (extra surprising since I assumed the error was related to `h` being a `factor`.

That's as far as I've gotten... it certainly seems like a bug somewhere. This is a pain because the `cache`d chunk takes about 20 minutes to run -- a perfect use case for only running it on occasion if the underlying code changes. But as stands this isn't feasible.

title: Changes to environments with `with()` are not cached
description:
It would appear that changes to an `environment` object made with `with()` are not cached:

    ```{r}
    foo <- new.env()
    ```

    ```{r, cache=TRUE}
    with(foo, bar <- 42)
    ```

    ```{r}
    foo$bar
    ```

This will print 42 the first time it is run, and `NULL` afterwards.

I'm not sure if this is a bug (it could be argued that `with()` is a function called for its side-effects) but I'm experimenting with the idea of collecting all analysis results in a set of `environment`s, and it would be great if this would play nicely with `knitr`' s cache.

title: Highlight in-line and chunk outputs for review (feature request)
description:
I work in a tightly-regulated environment. Before they can be exported from a  secure environment, all results must be checked by a third party to ensure that there is no danger of breaching privacy.
Checking results is a significant burden on the service.
If we are able to introduce knitr into this workflow it would help. This is because with knitr the output is intrinsically more concise and is usually given with some context which will help the checkers.
Would it be possible to introduce a package option which allows us to toggle between highlighting/not highlighting in-line and chunk outputs? This would make it easier for the checker to see what is and isn't results. 

The following gives example source code and output,
source:
In 1999, there were `r nrow(my_data)` patients.
output for checking:
In 1999, there were **`15,433`** patients.
final output once checked:
In 1999, there were 15,433 patients.

title: Unneeded warnings  when creating plot using non-default fonts
description:
Take this code snippet as an example (assuming "Ubuntu" font is installed in the system):

```
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}

<<dev='png'>>=
library(ggplot2)
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=mpg, y=wt), data=mtcars) +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 16, family = "Ubuntu"))
@

\end{document}
```

When compiling this with knitr, the output pdf will contain a long list of warnings similar as below:

```
## Warning: font family 'Ubuntu' not found in PostScript font database
```

However, if we call the device function directly,

```
png()
library(ggplot2)
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=mpg, y=wt), data=mtcars) +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 16, family = "Ubuntu"))
dev.off()
```

then there is no such warning issued.

I believe this is caused by the null graphics device `pdf(NULL)`. From my understanding knitr will evaluate code chunk on this null device and record the plotting operations to some objects. However, `pdf()` only support standard fonts like "Times" and "Courier", and will yell to other fonts that it does not recognize.

The "real" null device mentioned in http://yihui.name/en/2010/12/a-special-graphics-device-in-r-the-null-device/ is already removed from R. Is there any other approach to solve this problem?

title: The chunk option 'render=' is missing on the knitr web site.
description:
I was searching for a way to print data.frames as nicely formatted tables per default in knitr. 

During the research, following the source code of `knitr::knit` and the functions it calls, I learned that I simply can override the `knitr::knit_print` S3 function to archieve a custom printing for certain file types. 

My main point is, that I would have found the right way to do it much quicker, if the knitr home page, https://yihui.name/knitr/options/, would list the `render=` option, which is closely related to this problem. It's currently not listed.  The help page of `knitr::knit_print` is the only place where I saw the `render=` chunk option being mentioned. Also the help of `knitr::opts_chunk` where I also looked to get a list of available chunk options, simply references the web site without the `render=` option. 

As far as I understood it, the `render=` chunk option is a great way to customize the output for one chunk alone or a few chunks, independent of the result type being printed. I therefore would like to propose that this option is also listed on the home page. 

A short paragraph, which simply redirects to the correct help pages and vignettes would be enough:

> * `render`: (`knitr::knit_print`; `function(x, ..., inline = FALSE, options = list()`) the function which formats the result of the chunk for the final output format. The function is given `x`, the object to be printed, as well as optionally, the arguments `inline` and `options`. Type in R `vignette('knit_print', package = 'knitr')` and `?knitr::knit_print` for more information.

title: knit_filter() throws error for markdown input
description:
Running `knit_filter()` on R markdown input does not work:
 
``` r
library(knitr)
packageVersion("knitr")
#> [1] '1.19'
fname <- tempfile(fileext = ".Rmd")
writeLines(c("---", "---"), con = fname)
knit_filter(fname)
#> Error in gsub(p$inline.code, "", x[m == 2]): invalid regular expression '(?<!(^|
#> )``)`r[ #]([^`]+)\s*`', reason 'Invalid regexp'
```

The underlying cause is a modification of the `inline.code` regexp for markdown documents introduced in #1416, which is a valid ICU pattern but not compatible with base regexps or PCRE. This change has caused problems before (see commit 138c634, also rstudio/blogdown#150) and is easily fixed e.g. by using `stringr::str_replace_all()` instead of `gsub()`.

I will gladly provide a PR for this simple change, but am seeking guidance as to how this should be handled:

- It seems that there is some redundancy: `knit_filter()` needs to identify code and inline blocks just as with regular processing, and it seems that it has not caught up with e.g. the use of `knit_patterns`. Could it be possible to build `knit_filter()` based on existing functions like `R/parser.R:split_file()`, or is it desirable to keep it as a lightweight separate function?
- As far as I can tell, this is the only pattern that works with ICU engines but not PCRE. It can, however, be reformulated to comply with PCRE. The pattern documentation at [https://yihui.name/knitr/patterns/](https://yihui.name/knitr/patterns/) does not seem to dictate which flavour of regular expressions to use; I think it would be a good idea to use the same flavour for all patterns instead of treating a single one differently. Is this interesting/relevant enough to warrant opening another issue?
- Extending on the last point (pattern compatibility): There is another place in [`R/parser.R:parse_inline()`](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/1fda36f589545cd6922cd6cbdc9918e9fa778cfe/R/parser.R#L188) that treats `inline.code` as a base regexp. However, it is only executed if `inline.comment` is set, which is currently not the case for markdown patterns. Should this be changed to deal with ICU patterns (for consistency)?

title: Caching and knitr::knitr_exit()
description:
Hi, this is a super small issue, but  I thought I'd mention it anyway.  When running a long document, I use `knit_exit()` to run parts of it at a time.  Because some of the calculations take a long time, I use cache everything.

The issue seems to be how the `knit_exit()` command is cached.  The first time knitting the document, the it stops in the proper spot.  However if I knit again without editing the chunk where I call `knit_exit()`, it moves on to the rest of the document.

This should be able to be reproduced by running the following .Rmd twice (fixing the backticks closing the chunks, which had to be changed to render here), and comparing the output:

```r
---
title: "Early Exit Caching MWE"
---

```{r include=FALSE}
library(knitr)
opts_chunk$set(cache=TRUE)
``
Here is some text

```{r chunk1}
plot(x=1:10)
knitr::knit_exit()
``

a bit more text that I haven't finished writing, and don't want knitted yet

```{r chunk2}
# I am trying to debug this error, and dont want to knit it yet
plot(x=unassigned_variable)
``
```

The easy way to solve this is just to put the exit call in a chunk by itself, with caching disabled for that chunk. 

This may well be the desired behaviour, but I just thought I'd mention it!

Looking into the code I think I found the origin of the problem located in the `eng_dot` function of the `engines.r` file and especially in the following lines:

> cmd = sprintf(command_string, shQuote(**options$engine %n% options$engine.path**),
 >               shQuote(f), ext <- options$fig.ext %n% dev2ext(options$dev),
>shQuote(paste0(fig <- fig_path(), '.', ext)))

As `options$engine` is always defined, `options$engine.path` has no chance to be used!

One way to correct code is simply swapping `options$engine` and `options$engine.path` or use the function `get_engine_path(options$engine.path,options$engine)` you use for other engines.

title: Hardcoded dependency version for libicui18n (and others)?
description:
I had R Studio all up and working properly including being able to knit output files and then I went ahead and upgraded to Fedora 24. Apparently that upgraded 3 files from version 54 to version 56 that knitr required. It looks like it wasn't universally required at version 54 as other shared libraries were also upgraded to version 56 and that worked perfectly. As it stands right now, when I run

```
install.packages("knitr")

title: Some non-ASCII characters that exist in native encoding are wrongly encoded when knit()-ing
description:
When knit() a UTF-8 file (at least under Windows), some characters disappear under some circumstances. This seems to happen with characters that exist in the native encoding (windows-1252 on Windows) but non in latin1 (ISO-8859-1) or UTF-8, and only happens when printing the characters from R.

Here’s an example document, saved as UTF-8:

    \documentclass{article}
    \begin{document}
    
    æ, ø, å
    1–2
    
    <<>>=
    "æ, ø, å"
    "1–2"
    @
    
    \end{document}

When compiling this (using `knit2pdf("test.Rnw", encoding="UTF-8")`), the first two lines containing

    æ, ø, å
    1–2

are output correctly, but for the version created **inside the R chunk**, the output for the `1–2` string is wrongly encoded for the en-dash (–). The output for the `æ, ø, å` string is *correctly* encoded. One can check this using:

    library(readr)
    d = read_lines_raw("test.tex")
    d[c(64,70)]

which results in

    [[1]]
     [1] 23 23 20 5b 31 5d 20 22 c3 a6 2c 20 c3 b8 2c 20 c3 a5 22

    [[2]]
     [1] 23 23 20 5b 31 5d 20 22 31 c2 96 32 22

This is meant to represent

    [1] "æ, ø, å"
    [1] "1–2"

As you can see, the en-dash is encoded as `c2 96`. The correct encoding in UTF-8 would be `e2 80 93`. (And the correct encoding in the native encoding, windows 1252, is `96`.) The *first* time the string occurs, i.e., outside the R chunk, it *is* correctly encoded:

    > d[56]
    [[1]]
    [1] 31 e2 80 93 32

Note that the en-dash is one of the rare characters that are *not* available in latin1 (ISO 8859-1) but *are* available in the native Windows encoding (Windows-1252, AKA cp1252). These are the letters listed in red in this image at Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows-1252

The encoding problems seems to happen all of these characters. For example, `“` is written as `c2 93` by knitr. The Windows-1252 encoding would be `93`, while the *correct* UTF-8 encoding would be `e2 80 9c`. So it seems like the Windows-1252 encoding is used, but prefixed by `c2`, for some reason.

In summary, characters that exist in Windows-1252 (my native encoding) but *not* in ISO 8859-1 are wrongly encoded if and only if they occur in the *output* of R commands.

This bug is possibly related to the older (and fixed) #1094.

title: Floating TOC in HTML docs doesn't highlight scrollable sections
description:
When creating an HTML Rmarkdown document with a floating TOC, and some of the output from the cells in the middle of the sections are scrollable tables, when passing through those sections (when scrolling), the TOC no longer updates itself to reflect that one is browsing those sections (that contain scrollable tables).

**Steps to reproduce:**
* Create an Rmarkdown document with a float TOC, e.g.
``` yaml
---
title: "rmd doc"
output:
  html_document:
    theme: united
    toc: yes
    toc_float:
      collapsed: no
---
```
* Create some code chunk that would output a scrollable HTML table, e.g.
``` R
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
df <- data.frame(col1 = c(1,2,3), col2= c('a', 'b', 'c'))
kable(df) %>% kableExtra::kable_styling() %>% scroll_box(height = "500px")
```
* Put that code under some header in the middle of the document, with more headers above.
* Scroll through the document and watch the TOC at the side.

**Expected beahvior:**
* TOC should highlight the section that the user is browsing.

**Actual behavior:**
* When browsing the scrollable sections, it keeps on highlighting whatever was being highlighted before.

**Reproducible:** always, with different web browsers.

**Setup:** R version 3.5.0, knitr version 1.20.

title: knit_params mangles UTF-8 text not representable in current locale
description:
Small reprex:

```r
Sys.setlocale(locale = "English")
contents <- "---\nparams:\n  test: '\u4f60\u597d'\n---\n"  # 你好
Encoding(contents) <- "UTF-8"
print(contents)
knitr::knit_params(contents)
```

The generated parameter for `test` is replaced with its UTF-8 code point:

```r
> knitr::knit_params(contents)
$`test`
$`value`
[1] "<U+4F60><U+597D>"

$name
[1] "test"

attr(,"class")
[1] "knit_param"
```

From what I can see, this occurs because `split_lines()` attempts to (unintentionally) re-encode text into the active locale. Some options given the implementation here:

https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/0a9a502c809e0d38a987ef8934148c1304a939ce/R/utils.R#L605-L611

1. Use `textConnection(x, encoding = "bytes")` and then re-mark the encoding after reading from the connection,

2. Use `strsplit()`, but handle the special case where `x` is an empty string.

@yihui let me know if you have a preference here and I can try to put together a PR.

title: wrap_rmd breaks inline code
description:
I am working on a paper with R Markdown (processing to PDF with pdflatex). I am doing the analyses in a separate R script and then including results in the paper with a reference to the variable name from my analyses. In this case, `wrap_rmd` breaks inline code.

For example, "Analysis.R" is a script with the following code: `an.example.variable.name <- 1`. "Paper.Rmd" is as follows:
````r
---
title: "Untitled"
output: pdf_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
source("Analysis.R")
```

## Introduction

This is an example paragraph illustrating how knitr::wrap_rmd will break `r an.example.variable.name` because it is inline code.
````

If I knit that file as is, all is well. If I do `knitr::wrap_rmd("Paper.Rmd")` and knit the result, then the inline code includes a line break and the output is incorrect.

If I have the analysis code within the markdown file, however, it seems this is not an issue. In my current case, though, it is a lot cleaner to have all of the analyses in a separate script and bring in results as needed in the markdown file, so I'm hoping to avoid the solution, "Just put all of your analysis code in the markdown file."

title: Error in knit2html when called from Rmd file on rstudio.cloud because default chunk options are missing
description:
Dear Yihui,

I encountered a very strange bug when using `knitr::knit2html` on the `rstudio.cloud`. It took me quite some time to get to the core of the problem in a simple example. But here it is.

In the following rstudio.cloud project

[https://rstudio.cloud/project/46324](https://rstudio.cloud/project/46324)

There is the R file `knitr_test.R` with the following code:

library(knitr)
txt = "```{r 'test_chunk'}\n1+1\n```"

html

knitr::opts_chunk$get()
