title: knitr does not seem to set inline argument for knit_print() methods
description:
I want to write a custom `knit_print.classFoo` method which behaves differently when called from within inline R and proper knitr chunks.

I studied the [custom print methods vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/knitr/vignettes/knit_print.html), and came across the following relevant example:

```
knit_print.classC = function(x, inline = FALSE, ...) {
  # different output according to inline=TRUE/FALSE
  if (inline) {
    'inline output for classC'
  } else {
    'chunk output for classC'
  }
}
```

This, along with the surrounding description let me to the hypothesis that when knitr "runs" a chunk with the default `render` chunk option (`knitr::render()`), knitr would somehow pass on to the above `knit_print.classC()` method whether it was currently being run from `inline` or not.

So my **expected** behavior was that:
- I could define some knit_print.classFoo(x, inline, ...) {...} *without* specifying an `inline = FALSE` default, because knitr would always supply this argument anyway
- When evaluated inside a) a knitr chunk and b) inline r (`r knit_print(foo)`), I would see *different* results, based something akin to the above if/else logic.

Both of these turn out not to be true.
Without a default `inline` argument, a `knit_print.classFoo()` method fails with:

```
Error in knit_print.psGrid(x, ...) : 
  argument "inline" is missing, with no default
```

Also, when calling `knit_print(foo)` **explicitly* inside a) a knitr chunk and b) inline r, the two instances would produce different results based on the if/else logic, but they don't.
Instead, both invocations seem to fall back on the default `inline = FALSE` yielding the *same* results in both cases.

Did I get this right, and is there some problem here?
Or am I misunderstanding the whole design?

I'd be happy to amend the vignette with a PR to clarify this.

In my case, I've got my project directory, which has subdirectories `docs/`, `data/`, `src/`, and so on. title: Setting a knit_hook can change other default hooks
description:
Here is some output that is correct: ```r library(knitr) res <- knit2html( text = c("```{r}", "a <- 1", "# A comment", "a * 2", "```"), fragment.only = TRUE ) cat(res) # 
a <- 1
# # A comment
# a * 2
#
# # 
## [1] 2
#
``` However, if you use `knit_hooks$set()` before calling `knit2html()`, you get something different. ```r library(knitr) knit_hooks$set(evaluate = evaluate::evaluate) res <- knit2html( text = c("```{r}", "a <- 1", "# A comment", "a * 2", "```"), fragment.only = TRUE ) cat(res) #

a <- 1# A commenta * 2## [1] 2

``` I believe this behavior is caused by this code: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/7386aa39/R/output.R#L251-L254 This is causing a problem on shinyapps.io and RSC, because they call `knit_hooks$set(evaluate = evaluate::evaluate)`. Here's an example of an app that is broken: https://winston.shinyapps.io/020-knit-html/ cc @aronatkins @trestletech

title: Tangled R file has trailing whitespaces
description:
When tangling an R-Markdown file that has `eval = FALSE` set, the corresponding block in the output file is the input with each line prepended with a comment marker and a whitespace. This results in lines with trailing whitespaces if the original block contains empty lines. Similar to #1049, trailing whitespaces can be annoying if an automated linting system flags them as errors (since they usually result from sloppiness).

Example:
````
```{r, eval = FALSE}
a

b
```
````
results in (I replaced trailing whitespace with underscores):
```
## ---- eval = FALSE-------------------------------------------------------
#  a
#__
#  b
```
(the output apparently differs slightly between going the `purl` route or using the knitr vignette engine that uses `hook_purl`)

The simplest workaround that I can see is to set all `eval = FALSE` blocks also to `purl = FALSE`, but it would be useful if this were the default behaviour, or if there were a simple setting to do this.

(The other solution I can see besides just firing up a script after `buildVignettes` is to basically re-implement `hook_purl` with a one line change within my document, which seems quite inelegant.)

title: Setting `out.width` without `out.height` will not enlarge smaller images (pdf)
description:
Sorry - I am not quite sure if this is an rmarkdown bug or knitr bug. It is to do with the rmarkdown latex template, but it's a knitr option.

If

* pdf (latex) output
* specify `out.width` on a chunk
* include a graphic that is smaller than the `out.width`,

then

* the image is not resized larger

(when compiling using `rmarkdown::render`).

## example

~~~
---
title: "test"
output:
  pdf_document:
    keep_tex: true
---

First I create an image with imagemagick.

```
convert magick:rose rose.png
```

It is 70x46 pixels.

Then I include it using `knitr::include_graphics` at its normal size

```{r, fig.cap="Rose at its usual size"}
knitr::include_graphics('rose.png')
```

Then I scale it up to be 50% linewidth (as an aside, I need to escape the % symbol
in the fig.cap).

```{r, fig.cap="Rose at 50\\% linewidth", out.width='50%'}
knitr::include_graphics('rose.png')
```

It does not change in size. I have to set the height also.

```{r, fig.cap="Rose at 50\\% linewidth and textheight", out.width='50%', out.height='\\textheight'}
knitr::include_graphics('rose.png')
```
~~~

## expected output

The second image should be 50% of the line width (enlarged).

## actual output

The second image is still the original size, 70x46.

## details

On examining the `.tex` file, the LaTeX is fine. There is a 

```
\includegraphics[width=0.5\linewidth]{rose} \caption{Rose at 50\% linewidth}\label{fig:unnamed-chunk-2}
```

so the `0.5\linewidth` is being propagated correctly.

## why

It seems to be to do with the `\maxwidth` and `\maxheight` in the rmarkdown latex template (e.g. `~/R/library/3.3/rmarkdown/rmd/latex/default-1.17.0.2.tex`): the code that stops the images from overflowing the page by setting the default options to `width=\maxwidth, height=\maxheight, keepaspectratio`.

This sets the default width, height to the width, height of the input image (ie 70x46). 
Then I set `out.width='50%'` so we get height=46 pixels, width=0.5\linewidth.
However `keepaspectratio` keeps the image so it fits in the supplied dimensions, so it keeps the height to 46 pixels and doesn't resize it.

## fix

To fix it you have to set the out.height to \textheight (or something large) so that the image is properly enlarged. Perhaps this is not a bug, but at the very least it is unintuitive and not mentioned anywhere in the documentation for chunk options `out.width` and `out.height`.

For me (if I don't want to remember to set `out.height` to some guessed value every time I set `out.width`) I can fix it by adjusting the template (in the rmarkdown package)

```
\setkeys{Gin}{width=\maxwidth,height=\maxheight,keepaspectratio}
```

to

```
\setkeys{Gin}{width=\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio}
```

Then smaller images will be enlarged and larger images will be shrunk.
However I do not know if this will have unintended consequences, like making images overflow the margins or something. If I make this change have a chunk with no `out.width` and no `out.height`, the image is not enlarged to the whole page size, but maybe that doesn't hold in general.

Alternatively, add a note to the `out.width`/`out.height` chunk option documentation to explain that if `out.width` is set and the image is smaller, you must also set `out.height` (to something large) in order for the image to be enlarged.

## package details

I have this problem with rmarkdown 1.8.5, knitr 1.17.20.

However I also had it with whatever the current versions are with R 3.3 (from CRAN). Sorry, I do not have the specific version numbers, because I (incorrectly) thought this was a pandoc problem so updated my local pandoc to 2.0.x, which prompted me to have to update rmarkdown (which went to 1.8.5) and I updated knitr with devtools while I was at it, and forgot to note the previous version numbers.

I suspect any rmarkdown that uses the `\setkeys{Gin}{width=\maxwidth,height=\maxheight,keepaspectratio}` will have this problem.

## Aside

I did not realise that percent signs in `fig.cap` should be escaped for LaTeX (or else it thinks they are a comment) though it makes sense. I had assumed knitr would do it for me. Perhaps add a little note in the `fig.cap` documentation about this?

title: [Enquiry/Discussion] Design behind the tool
description:
Dear @yihui, thank you for this package, it helped me to create reproductive research during my PhD. Hope you are well.

The files I create with knitr are usually for my personal use, usually experiment logs to be saved in the project directory. For more complex documents (like my own thesis or a book I recently published) I tend to use a combination of gnumake and pandoc. Knitr is as powerful as these tools, but I keep coming back to them because of one feature. 

With make and pandoc I can organize the project better. The main aspect of this organization is that I can clearly separate style (cls, tex templates, doc templates, filters, etc) from contents (md files). This makes so much sense, because I can drop the style files in the style directory and my makefile takes care of running pandoc with the proper flags.

I understand where knitr comes from, its design is partially inherited from Sweave and that is fine. However, working in large documents causes the project directory to become cluttered with sources, intermediate files and the output. Style, contents and build objects are all present in the same directory.

I don't know if any of this makes sense to you. I was also a LyX user in the past, but after pandoc + make + sublime text I come less and less to LyX, as writing files is made so much easier and simpler. My makefile is publicly available [here](https://github.com/lf-araujo/mighty_make).

This made me think that perhaps knitr would benefit of a bit of this design pattern, by simply allowing the user to set the directory where source is to be found, where intermediate files should be saved (a hidden directory preferably) and where the output should be printed. Also, as an extra, load filters, templates and the cls automatically, following some heuristic.

- Does knitr already offer any of these functionalities? 
- If not, is it a good idea to incorporate a bit of folder management (I am sure there is a proper name for this type of programming pattern)?

Regards,

title: output path is not quoted in the cmd call to pandoc
description:
I am calling `knitr::pandoc` on a file whose path contains spaces. Sadly quite common on Windows.

Example:
> knitr::pandoc("C:/Users/Antoine Sachet/Projects/reprex/Introduction.md")
```
executing pandoc   -t html -o C:/Users/Antoine Sachet/Projects/reprex/Introduction.html "C:/Users/Antoine Sachet/Projects/reprex/Introduction_utf8.md"
pandoc.exe: Sachet/Projects/reprex/Introduction.html: openBinaryFile: does not exist (No such file or directory)
Error in (function (input, input_utf8, format, ext, cfg)  : 
  conversion failed
```

This happens because the output path passed to pandoc (`-o` argument) is not quoted so the space is messing things up.

I have tracked it to the following bit of code in `knitr:::pandoc_one`. Is there any reason why `out` is not quoted in `cmd` below while `input_utf8` is?

    cmd = paste("pandoc", pandoc_arg(cfg), pandoc_arg(cmn), "-t", 
        format, "-o", out, paste(shQuote(input_utf8), collapse = " "))

I figured there might have been a good reason not to use `shQuote(out)` instead of `out`? If not, I am happy to raise a PR.

title: Sass / SCSS language engine?
description:
Would there be interest in a PR for a [Sass / SCSS](https://sass-lang.com/) language engine? Sass is a CSS extension language which allows users to write CSS more efficiently / programatically and then convert it back to CSS.

Tactically, this would look similar to a `css` chunk. Where this chunk in RMarkdown:

```
{scss echo = FALSE}
$font-stack:    Helvetica, sans-serif
$primary-color: #00FF00

body
  font: 100% $font-stack
  color: $primary-color
```

Turns into this in-line CSS code:

```
<style type="text/css">
body {
  font: 100% Helvetica, sans-serif;
  color: #99badd;
}
</style>
```

However, behind the scenes, it's slightly more complicated than the `css` engine, since first the code is passed to the `sass` executable, and then that output subsequently receives treatment similar to `eng_html_asset()`. 

---

As I see it, potential pros include:

- since Sass / SCSS "feels" more like a programming language, it might appeal to R users
- similar to the existing `css` engine, this can help code be more self-contained
- a built-in Sass engine ensures code updates are captured (versus having a stand-alone Sass file which users must remember the re-convert so RMarkdown reads in the correct CSS file)

However, I realize it might be unnecessary because:

- Sass is probably overkill for the level of in-line CSS used in most RMarkdowns
- Sass could already be run inside an RMarkdown via the Javascript engine (however, this requires more Javascript knowledge to set-up, and the Sass website states that it is slower) or called from the bash engine (however, this is true of many of the engines!)

Please let me know what you think! Just for fun, I was able to get an SCSS engine to work on Windows, but before I worry more about other systems or some issues specific to the Sass side, I thought I would see if it was of interest.

Thank you for such a great (family of) tool(s)!

title: kable produces malformed reference links after HTML calls in blogdown
description:
I have asked this question in [stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/54545733/kable-produces-malformed-reference-links-within-lapply-function-in-blogdown) too but did not get an answer yet.

The gist of it is, within a freshly created blogdown page, creating a table using `kable` causes the caption to be edited to include a reference link and a table count (eg. "Table 1: Intended Caption"). This is undesirable for me but I assume it is intended behaviour.

However this behaviour changes when `kable` is called from within pretty much anything that uses a `{`. The reference link is added by appending a `(\#tab:codeblocklabel)` in the beginning of each table which html just shows as plain text.

Here is an an example post that highlights the problem. Here `test1`'s caption is processed correctly but all the others use the `(\#tab:codeblocklabel)` format.


    ---
    title: test
    author: ''
    date: '2019-02-05'
    slug: test
    categories: []
    tags: []
    ---
   
    ```{r setup, include=FALSE}
    knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE)
    ```
    
    ```{r test1}
    library(knitr)
    library(magrittr)
    library(kableExtra)
    library(shiny)
    
    data.frame(a= c(1,2,3)) %>% kable(caption = 'test',format = 'html')
    
    ```

    ```{r test2}
    
    lapply(1:2,function(x){
        data.frame(a= c(1,2,3)) %>% kable(caption = 'test2',format = 'html') %>% HTML()
    }) -> tables
    
    tables[[1]]
    
    tables[[2]]
    ```


    ```{r test3}
    for(i in 1){
      table = data.frame(a= c(1,2,3)) %>% kable(caption = 'test3',format = 'html') %>% HTML()
    }
    table
    ```

    ```{r test4}
    {data.frame(a= c(1,2,3)) %>% kable(caption = 'test4',format = 'html') %>% HTML()}
    ```

As stated on the stackoverflow I was able to identify the code that causes this behaviour in the `create_label` function but could not understand how "bookdown.internal.label" is set or can be modified.

Ultimately, I don't want my captions to be edited by kintr at all. But the second behaviour is clearly wrong and unintentional while the first is probably a sensible default (though I would appreciate some hints in getting rid of that too).

title: Include travis folding markers
description:
When building large or many rmarkdown files on travis (e.g. https://travis-ci.org/hadley/adv-r/jobs/476364254), it is hard to find problems because the log file is thousands of lines long. Travis provides a way to handle this through [folding markers](https://github.com/travis-ci/travis-rubies/blob/9f7962a881c55d32da7c76baefc58b89e3941d91/build.sh#L38-L44) (these are undocumented but used by all build systems so can not change).  

I think it would be very useful if knitr detected that it was being called in travis (by checking the TRAVIS env var), and inserting the folding comments at the start and end of each document.

title: xcolor option clash with fancyvrb v 3.0.
description:
Hi,

A couple of my packages were showing `! LaTeX Error: Option clash for package xcolor` error in CRAN recently. I was not able to reproduce it until I received an email from Prof. Brian Ripley which informed that this was because of the updated `fancyvrb` Tex package. I was using the following option with conflicted with `xcolor` being called by `fancyvrb` later.

```
header-includes:
- \usepackage[table]{xcolor}
``` 

He suggested a adding `\PassOptionsToPackage{table}{xcolor}` to the tex file before the  `\documentclass` line. when I manualy do that, it is fixed, but with `render::rmarkdown()`, it is not working.


A minimal reprex is given as follows:


```````
---
title: "Test"
author: "author1, author2"
date: "14 November 2018"
header-includes:
- \usepackage[table]{xcolor}
output:
  pdf_document:

vignette: |

title: [Feature Request] `knit` `.Rmd` with `params` in yaml header to `.md`
description:
### Issue
---
`rmarkdown::render` works nicely on a Rmarkdown file with `params` (https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/params-declare.html).

`knitr::knit(<Rmd-file>, <md-file>)` however **appears to fail to make use of `params`** and will produce something like below in the respective chunks that try to make use of `params`:

```r
## Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos): object 'params' not found
```

### Background
---
We have a workflow to publish news posts on our website that generates website-compatible `.md` files from an initial `.Rmd` document, which is our preferred source format for posts.

### Workaround
---
A possible work-around is to **use a hook**:
```r
paramHook <- function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) {
    if (!exists("params", envir = envir)) {
        params <- eval(parse(text = knitr:::.knitEnv$tangle.params[2]))
        assign("params", params, envir = envir)
    }
  }
}
knitr::knit_hooks$set(doPar = paramHook)
knitr::knit(<Rmd-file>, <md-file>)
```
This **requires adding e.g. `doPar = 1`** as chunk option to those chunks that make use of params.

I think it's clear that this work-around is not very nice and it seems I shouldn't have to do it.

### Considerations
---
It is maybe not a trivial request. One possibility I could see without touching too much code is to modify `knitr:::process_file`:
```r
process_file <- function(text, output)
{
  groups = split_file(lines = text)
  if (isTRUE(opts_knit$get("yaml.pars"))) {
    parList = list(label = "yaml-params", include = FALSE)
    knit_code$set(`yaml-params` = structure(
      .knitEnv$tangle.params, chunk_opts = parList
    ))
    groups = c(
      groups[1],
      list(structure(list(params = parList), class = "block")),
      groups[-1]
    )
  }
  n = length(groups)
  <.......................>
```
Requires **`opts_knit$set(yaml.pars = TRUE)`**.

Doesn't look very nice either, but here is where I'm sure you'll have an opinion.

title: `format_sci`: `\cdot` instead of `\times`
description:

Is there a reason, why the `\times` ("×")sign is preferred over the (as far as I know more commonly used) dot ("·", typeset by LaTeX's `\cdot` macro)?

title: Chunk option `fig.align` causes image tags to be created in .html
description: I frequently write Rmd files in RStudio and then `knit` them using the built in `knitHTML` button. Occasionally I like to produce something other than an html file from my code though. For this, I use `pandoc()` to convert the markdown file that is produced with each click of the `knitHTML` button into some other document type (mostly .docx files). I always set several chunk options globally at the beginning of each Rmd document I create, like so: ``` opts_chunk$set(comment=NA, fig.height=8, fig.width=7, fig.align='center') ``` This always resulted in normal markdown-style image tags in the knitted .md file. An example: ``` ![plot of chunk BoxPlots](Some_Path/BoxPlots.png) ``` I noticed this was no longer the case after updating to the most recent version of `knitr` because when I called `pandoc()` to convert my .md file to a .docx, no images appeared in the resulting Word file. After some exploration I found that my images were now html tagged in the .md file. An example: ``` ``` This is what was causing my images to no longer appear in my converted Word files. I traced this back to the chunk option `fig.align`. If I remove this setting from my global chunk settings at the beginning of the document, all of my image tags are as they should be and the .md file converts to .docx perfectly. If I set the option for just one chunk, the figure tag(s) produced by that chunk are .html tags and all of the other figure tags are markdown-style. I realize that setting this option makes no difference in the resulting .md file, so you might make the argument "Why are you using it anyway?", but I don't ignore the .html file produced. I'd like to be able to specify how the .html file appears and still be able to convert the .md file to some other file format if need be. Also, I had code that "worked" and after installing the new package, it "broke", so I thought I might help some others having this issue. Thanks for the great package!

title: Minor suggestion (with .diff) which allows to run scripts on the knit()ed .tex
description:
Suggestion for improvement (of ./R/header.R): Replace %% by % on line 126 and 127, see the following `.diff` (which I would have attached as a file if that file type was supported... do you prefer `.diff.zip`?). 

--- header.R	2018-01-02 11:48:28.000000000 -0500
+++ header_new.R	2019-03-23 09:22:03.000000000 -0400
@@ -123,8 +123,8 @@
 '
 
 .header.maxwidth =
-'%% maxwidth is the original width if it is less than linewidth
-%% otherwise use linewidth (to make sure the graphics do not exceed the margin)
+'% maxwidth is the original width if it is less than linewidth
+% otherwise use linewidth (to make sure the graphics do not exceed the margin)
 \\makeatletter
 \\def\\maxwidth{ %
   \\ifdim\\Gin@nat@width>\\linewidth

The reason for this suggestion is that this is (seems to be) the only comment that's introduced in the knitted `.tex` which starts with two '%%' -- and that messes up scripts which grab (= grep) for that (there are various reasons why one would want to run such scripts on the generated `.tex`, I can give more details if necessary).

title: Temp file engine
description:
I would like to propose a `temp` language engine for `knitr` which would place the code in its chunk into a temp file, named according to a user-specified `temp.filename` chunk option. 

I've pasted an example of usage at the bottom of this issue. In summary, the resulting filepath of the chunk content would then be `paste0(tempdir(), '\\', {{user-specified temp.filename}})`. For convenience, the engine would also assign a character of this path to the variable called `{{user-specified temp.filename minus extension}}_filepath` in the `global_knit()` environment.

This would help reduce the necessity to write "ugly" boilerplate code of assigning file contents to a character string, creating a temp file path, and writing characters to a file. Personally, I would particularly appreciate this when I'm writing and reading YAML into R. 

If this is of interest, I have a PR mostly ready to go. (I was curious to try to implement it regardless, so it was a fine use of time even if it's not of interest for `knitr` :slightly_smiling_face:) But it felt more polite to float the idea as an issue first, per the Contributing guidelines. 

Thanks for your time and consideration!

The following code is a mock-up RMarkdown to show what writing and reading temp files with this engine would look like. I picked a trivial example to make it clear what the engine is doing, but admittedly this specific application (writing R code to a temp file to `source()` back in) isn't particularly useful:

````
---
title: "Temp File Examples"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

## Examples

```{temp temp.filename = 'script.R'}
my_function <- function(x){ x+1 }
```

```{r}
script_filepath
```


```{r}
source(paste0(tempdir(),'\\','script.R'))
my_function(5)
rm(my_function)
```

```{r}
source(fs::path(tempdir(), 'script.R'))
my_function(5)
rm(my_function)
```

```{r}
source(script_filepath)
my_function(5)
rm(my_function)
```


````

title: Reliance on dvisvgm file naming leads to issues with tikz engine
description:
First, thanks so much for knitr!

I am using the tikz engine with the svg suffix. The knitr code seems to rely on dvisvgm creating a file with a .svg suffix, which is later relocated to the appropriate directory:
```
if (system2('dvisvgm', fig) != 0) stop('Failed to compile ', fig, ' to ', fig2)
 file.rename(basename(fig2), fig2)
```
Unfortunately, dvisvgm creates files without the .svg suffix when the chunk name already has a period in it, leading to an error message, e.g. `cannot rename file 'chunk.name-1.svg' to 'bug01-1_files/figure-html/chunk.name-1.svg', reason 'No such file or directory'`. My immediate solution is not to use periods in the chunk name. A possible solution in knitr would be not count on dvisvgm naming convention, and redirect its output explicitly to the correct file: rather than use `dvisvgm filename`, use `paste("dvisvgm -s", fig, ">", basename(fig2))` (I did not test the proposed code).

Sample chunk:

     ```{tikz chunk.name, fig.ext="svg"}
     \usetikzlibrary{arrows}
     \begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=2cm, auto,>=latex', thick, scale = 0.5]
     \end{tikzpicture}
     ```

Thanks again!

- ucp

title: `include_graphics` output not suppressed by `fig.show='hide'`
description:
The `bookdown` docs sold me on the value of `include_graphics`. There, it says:

> The syntax for controlling the image attributes is the same as when images are generated from R code, e.g., chunk options fig.cap, out.width, and fig.show still have the same meanings.

However, `fig.show='hide'` does not appear to suppress the figure output. See below for a reproducible example (I installed the latest CRAN version of `knitr` before running).

My use-case: I want images to appear in the PDF output but be substituted by "[Insert Figure Here]" in the Word output. To achieve this, I wrote a `knit_hook` which flips the `fig.show` switch and pastes in the necessary text. Unfortunately, this doesn't work for chunks where I call `include_graphics`, because `fig.show` won't suppress the image.

````
---
title: "suppress include_graphics output"
output: html_document
---

```{r, fig.show='hide'}
library(knitr)
knitr::include_graphics('https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Eastern_Grey_Squirrel.jpg/290px-Eastern_Grey_Squirrel.jpg')
```

```{r, fig.show='hide'}
x <- rnorm(10)
y <- rnorm(10)
plot(x, y)
```

title: R package structure block chunk cache functionnality
description:
Hello,

I discover an issue that I can't explain with `knitr` cache for chunks. If I compile your cache example [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yihui/knitr-examples/master/056-huge-plot.Rmd](url) in any classic folder it works perfectly. But as soon as I compile the example in a _vignettes_ folder inside a R package project, the cache is updated at each run even if the code doesn't change. So in conclusion it render the cache option unusable inside a package. 

The only solution I got for the moment is to work on my vignette outside from the package structure, and to copy paste the new vignette inside the package whenever I want to save my changes.

I think it may be linked to some automatic procedure affecting the files inside a package structure due to R-studio. I tried both in a package with a git repository or without git and the conclusion is git is not responsible for this. Last thing I noticed that outside from a package a folder _Example_files_ is created in addition of _Example_cache_ but not inside a package structure. So does that mean that the package structure is blocking the file cache, and that's why the cache option doesn't work ?

Thanks for your time and your great package

title: A LaTeX warning destroys citations
description:
Problem described in the following LaTeX code say in a `MyVignette.Rnw` file

```
\documentclass{article}

\title{A \LaTeX{} warning destroys citations} \author{}

\begin{document}
This illustrates a minor problem met with \verb@knitr::knit2pdf@ when
trying to bibcite something like \cite{myCitation} but getting "?". 

\label{Foo} \label{Foo}

In this \LaTeX{} code, the label \texttt{Foo} is multiply defined,
which produces a warning. If we proceed the file with
\verb@knitr::knit2pdf@ the citation does not appear as it should, and
a misleading warning concerning the citation is shown. So \LaTeX{}
warnings can break the knitr-ing process. By compiling the
\texttt{.tex} file generated by \textbf{knitr}, using bibtex and then
compiling \textit{twice}, the citation reappears normally: only the
warning on the multiple label remains.

Of course, by simply changing the second label into \texttt{Bar},
everything is OK.

\bibliographystyle{apalike}
\bibliography{myBiblio}
\end{document}
```

To be used with the following content for the `myBiblio.bib` file

```
@article{myCitation,
     title = "{How to be cited in a knitr Vignette}",
     author = {Someone, M},
     journal = {A Very Interesting Journal},
     year = {2019}
}
```

title: Chunk option out.width triggers escaped LaTeX commands instead of figures in LaTeX/pdf output
description:
Dear Yihui Xie,

thank you for your great work with knitr. I have found a small problem when creating LaTeX/pdf from Rmd, which I would think should be fixed in the knitr-part of the pipeline.

Start with the following Rmd file and try to translate it with `rmarkdown::render`:

````rmd
---
title: "Untitled"
author: "Stephan Struckmann"
date: "8/12/2019"
output: latex_document
---

```{r out.width=c('100%%')}
plot(cars)
```

```{r}
plot(cars)
```
````

`r rmarkdown::render("Untitled.Rmd")` will then produce a file with the following lines in:

```latex
\textbackslash includegraphics{[}width=100\%\%{]}\{Untitled\_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-2-1\}

\includegraphics{Untitled_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-5-1.pdf}
```

The first line shows the error, the second displays that it is related to the chunk-option `out.width`.

I've already boiled this down to the pandoc-version. Pandoc escapes code now, I could not exactly find out, from which version on, but I suspect the 2.0.0-major release. I've already played around a bit with older versions.

The chunk option `out.width` however makes knitr writing plain LaTeX code to the intermediate *.knit.md file, which is then converted to a damaged tex by newer pandoc-versions. 

The intermediate file `Untitled.knit.md` contains the following rows:

````markdown
\includegraphics[width=100%%]{Untitled_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-2-1} 
![](Untitled_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-5-1.pdf)<!-- --> 
````

Older pandocs had simply passed through the LaTeX code before. I don't see an obvious work-around so far. Maybe, pandoc can somehow be forced to the old behavior, or some post-processing of the pandoc-created intermediate tex file could help. 

I would be available to assist with fixing this bug, if desired.

Anyway thank you for this great package,

Stephan

title: Support `fig.show='hold'` for office output
description:
When output is office formats (e.g., docx) and `fig.show='hold'`, then knitr coerces `fig.show='asis'` with warning.
This is introduced by https://github.com/yihui/knitr/commit/f6e3b62bf3090671fe47282a4f70b635df8368bb#diff-4910cdfe600c3874a655c6951e12daa0 to fix https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown/issues/249 and is expanded by https://github.com/yihui/knitr/commit/575e18e8961e16bee1595cca44ca7b93da006b82#diff-4910cdfe600c3874a655c6951e12daa0 .

However, regardless of the coercion, `fig.show='hold'` seems working.
In addition, removing the coercion still works.
I do not face error reported by https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown/issues/249 

Although I don't know what made things possible, can we remove the relevant lines?
If not, I think we should also add the treatment here: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/R/hooks-md.R#L20

## Example Rmd

````
---
title: "Untitled"
output :
  word_document: default
  powepoint_presentation: default
  odt_document: default
  rtf_document: default
  bookdown::word_document2: default
---

# fig.show='hold'

```{r base, fig.show='hold', fig.cap=.cap}
.cap = c('a', 'b')
plot(1)
'a'
plot(2)
```

# fig.show='asis'

```{r ref.label='base', fig.show='asis', fig.cap=.cap}

```
````

BTW, when `fig.show='hold'`, captions are not working in the above example.
I'm currently working to fix this.

title: kable: Vertical page position with "valign" option does behave faulty
description:
First, thank you for the great work!

I like to produce a floating table in `latex` with the `kable()`-function. Next to that I tried to figure out how the page position is set. There is an option 'valign' which comes from a hidden function `kable_latex` and is passed through when it is applied in `kable(dat,valign = "!b")`.

Producing a simple table we can do it like this:

```{r}
require(knitr)
dat <- data.frame(A=c(1,2,3,4),B=c(T,F))

kable(dat,format = "latex")
```
which will give the output as expected:
```
\begin{tabular}{r|l}
\hline
A & B\\
\hline
1 & TRUE\\
\hline
2 & FALSE\\
\hline
3 & TRUE\\
\hline
4 & FALSE\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
```
Putting a caption to the table, will generate a floating object with latex - `table` environment. But in case we like to have the table at the bottom of the page, which is usually done by `\begin{table}[!b]` the '[!b]' switch appears besides the ´tabular´ environment an NOT aside the ´table´. Proof:

R-code
```
require(knitr)
dat <- data.frame(A=c(1,2,3,4),B=c(T,F))

kable(dat,format = "latex",caption = "abc",valign = "!b")
```
And its output:
```
\begin{table} % <-- here [!b] is supposed to be

\caption{\label{tab:}abc}
\centering
\begin{tabular}[!b]{r|l}   %% here is the wrong position for [!b]
\hline
A & B\\
\hline
1 & TRUE\\
\hline
2 & FALSE\\
\hline
3 & TRUE\\
\hline
4 & FALSE\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
```
Since the functionality is given, but accidentally wrong composed, I would also suggest to document this option in the help of `kable` function.

title: [FR] kable_latex: support placement arguments
description:
Hi,

`knitr::kable_latex` does not "support" [float placement specifiers](https://tex.stackexchange.com/a/39019) diretly.
Placement specifiers are useful to gain more fine control about float placement on the page.
It should be easy to add to `knitr::kable_latex`, e.g.
```R
env1 = sprintf("\\begin{%s}%s\n", table.envir, table.argument)
```
where `table.argument` would default to `""`.
Then, a user could specify `kable(..., table.argument="[htp]")`, or more complex
things if not using the default "table" environment. 

This is, IMO, an improvement over the situation at the moment where it
is only possible adjust the default placement of all (`kable`) table,
e.g. `\makeatletter\renewcommand{\fps@table}{htp}\makeatother`.

I can provide a patch if desired.

Thanks,
Rasmus

title: Illegal unit of measure in pdf with fig.retina in bookdown::pdf_document2
description:
Using the `fig.retina` knitr option causes an "Illegal unit of measure" when trying to generate a pdf when the output is `bookdown::pdf_document2`.

It seems like in the intermediate `.tex` file, the `\includegraphics` just has a number for the width, but does not have a unit.
For example:
```
\includegraphics[width=720]{/home/dchen/Desktop/04-data-workflows/analysis/figures/demo-multi-1} \caption{The caption.}\label{fig:demo-multi}
```

but chaning it to

```
\includegraphics[width=720px]{/home/dchen/Desktop/04-data-workflows/analysis/figures/demo-multi-1} \caption{The caption.}\label{fig:demo-multi}
```
will let me run `pdflatex` to generate the pdf.

Minimal example:

This works:

````
---
output:
  bookdown::pdf_document2: default
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```
````

````
---
output:
  bookdown::pdf_document2: default

title: Cache dependencies
description:
Not sure if it is an issue with codetools or knitr (and where it should/could be "fixed") but:

```r
codetools::findGlobals(function(){x<-2*x})
```

doesn't return `x`.

The side effect is that, in the following, the "b" chunk does not depend on the "a" chunk. So changing the assignment in the "a" chunk will always report a result of `2`.

```r
<<knitr-config, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, results='hide'>>=
opts_chunk$set(cache=2, echo=FALSE, results='hide', autodep=TRUE)
@

<<a>>=
x <- 1
@

<<b>>=
x <- 2*x
@

<<res, results='asis'>>=

title: Pdf file too big (maybe compression?)
description:
Hi,

I have to plot around 500K points in several figures, and the files knitr is generating are too large. What follows is a small example reproducing the problem:

``` R
\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}

<<calc>>=
d <- data.frame(x=rnorm(500000, 0.1))
d$y <- d$x + rnorm(500000)
@

<<myplot, echo=FALSE, results='hide', out.width='\\linewidth'>>=
library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw()
print(p)
@

\end{document}
```

The generated PDF file is around 29MB. When I generate it by hand:

``` R
pdf('test.pdf')
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw()
print(p)
dev.off()
```

I get a PDF file with size 3.4MB. The files look equal. However, if I re-run the last code but using pdf device option 'compress=FALSE', I get a file with size ~30MB. That made me suspect that maybe knitr was calling with compression deactivated, but that seems strange, since that option is enabled by default.

Thank you for your amazing work. 

Regards,
Gus.

## Observed behavior

When `root.dir` is changed to a directory other than where the Rmd file is located, figures created by R and Python chunks are saved in different locations. Specifically, the R figures are saved relative to the location of the Rmd file, and the Python figures are saved relative to the working directory (i.e. the path specififed by `root.dir`).

## Expected behavior

According to the [online documentation for `fig.path`](https://yihui.org/knitr/options/#plots), the default value of `figure/` should be interpreted as a relative path for saving the figure files:

> if the prefix ends in a trailing slash, e.g. output/figures/, figures will be saved in the specified directory without any changes to filename prefix, thus providing a relative filepath alternative to the package-level option base.dir

It's unclear to me what it is relative to though. Since the Markdown file includes links starting with `figure/`, only the figure files created by the R chunks will be displayed.

Overall, I expect figure files to be saved in the same location regardless of the engine.

title: New width behaviour (version 1.26) invalidates cache
description:
This point is too general to warrant a specific example; rather it is a major effect of the 'minor' change in v. 1.26 with respect to the global `width` option. 

The `width` option is part of the MD5 sum for (in)validating the **knitr** cache, and thus any time users change the `width` option (e.g., to look at a particularly large nibble) and re-knit, they have -- probably inadvertently! -- invalidated their entire cache. This is a very easy mistake to make when working under Emacs/ESS instead of RStudio, and if there was a good reason to use caching, it is unfortunately also a very costly mistake.

Although it is always possible to work around this behaviour by setting `width` manually in a setup chunk, it feels like a dangerous 'gotcha', even for advanced users. Would it be possible to add the global `width` option to `knitr:::cache1.opts` somehow? That seems like it would fit the spirit of how `cache = 1` and `cache = 2` are intended to work.

title: Using spin() with langages other than R
description:
This is related to issues #1605 and #1773.  Because spin() relies on R's code parsing to identify multiline comments, no other language can be spun.

(I use an older version of spin() with Stata and SAS code, occasionally.)

For code  written wholly in another language, I propose the solution is to simply skip the R code parsing.  The cost is that spin will not recognize multiline comments **in languages other than R**.

description:

---

Hi,

We use Windows Server 2012 R2 for the [Bioconductor build system](https://bioconductor.org/checkResults/release/bioc-LATEST/) to build and check Bioconductor packages. When building the vignettes, we sometimes see a warning like this one for some packages:
```
Invalid Parameter - /figure-html
Warning in shell(paste(c(cmd, args), collapse = " ")) :
  'convert "overview_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png" -trim "overview_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png"' execution failed with error code 4
```
Tracking down this warning reveals at least 2 issues with knitr:
- The SystemRequirements field for knitr makes no mention of the dependency on ImageMagick.
- On Windows Server 2012 R2 (and maybe on other Windows flavors), if ImageMagick is not installed `Sys.which("convert")` returns: 
    ```
     > Sys.which("convert")
                                 convert
    "C:\\Windows\\SYSTEM32\\convert.exe"
    ```
    This `convert.exe` command is a Microsoft utility for converting a file-system from FAT to NTFS (see https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/convert). Unfortunately this is what `knitr::plot_crop()` picks up which is why we get the above warnings.

Since knitr already suggests CRAN package magick (since knitr 1.22), I wonder if there is any reason to not use this in `plot_crop()` instead of a system call to the `convert` command from ImageMagick. That way knitr would no longer depend on ImageMagick and the risk to pick up the wrong `convert` command would be eliminated, making `knitr::plot_crop()` more robust and platform independent.

Thanks,
H.

title: hook_pdfcrop misses plots
description:
If a chunk uses *multiple output devices* **and** *multiple plots*, `hook_pdfcrop()` will only crop a subset of the generated images.

Note that, despite its name, `hook_pdfcrop()` generally works for both png and pdf images (so should actually be called `hook_crop`).

## Reproducible example

Consider the following Rmd file, `barplots.Rmd` say:
````Rmd
```{r setup-knitr, include = FALSE}
library("knitr")
## be verbose about the files we crop
mockery::stub(hook_pdfcrop, "plot_crop", function(x) plot_crop(x, quiet = FALSE))
knit_hooks$set(crop = hook_pdfcrop)
```

## Example: barplot(1) triple

```{r barplot, echo = FALSE, dev = c("png","pdf"), crop = TRUE, out.width = "30%"}
barplot(1, main = "A")
barplot(1, main = "B")
barplot(1, main = "C")
```
````

Simply run `knit2html("barplots.Rmd", quiet = TRUE)` to see the problem:

```
cropping figure/barplot-1.png
cropping figure/barplot-2.pdf
PDFCROP 1.38, 2012/11/02 - Copyright (c) 2002-2012 by Heiko Oberdiek.
==> 1 page written on `figure/barplot-2.pdf'.
cropping figure/barplot-3.png
```

![snapshot](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4366501/67213038-9a367580-f41d-11e9-915c-32ca28a9c609.png)

In total, six image files are generated (3 pdf + 3 png), but only three of them are actually cropped:

file | cropped
---- | ----------
barplot-1.pdf | no
barplot-1.png | yes
barplot-2.pdf | yes
barplot-2.png | no
barplot-3.pdf | no
barplot-3.png | yes

## Bug

The bug is actually in the auxiliary function `all_figs` used by `hook_pdfcrop` (and `hook_png`):

https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/779f610d363d15e31dc914c9ca36af37d1bb6979/R/utils.R#L540-L543

In the above example, `ext = c("png", "pdf")` and `num = 3`, so the function will return the incomplete vector
```r
c("figure/barplot-1.png", "figure/barplot-2.pdf", "figure/barplot-3.png")
```
With strict `Sys.setenv("_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_" = TRUE)`, an error would occur from calling `fig_path()` this way since it expects its first argument to be of length one:
```
Error in suffix != "" && !grepl("[.]", suffix) : 
  'length(x) = 2 > 1' in coercion to 'logical(1)'
```

## Solution

I guess replacing the body of `all_figs` by something like
```r
unlist(lapply(X = ext, FUN = fig_path, options = options, number = seq_len(num)))
```
should fix the bug.

title: Possible bug with eval.after and fig.subcap
description:
I'm trying to use `eval.after` so that I can reference R objects in the subcaptions of a figure. The documentation suggests that `eval.after` should work for any chunk option, even though the example is always `fig.cap`. I'm using R 3.5.1 with knitr 1.2.0 from CRAN compiled from source. A MWE is below. I get the following error from the second chunk: `Error in paste("Mean =", mean_b) : object 'mean_b' not found`. If I delete the second code chunk and knit the file, everything is fine. I've also tried using subfig instead of subcaption with the redefined subfloat. Unless I've misunderstood the documentation, I think this is a bug.

```
\documentclass[12pt]{article}
\usepackage{subcaption}
\newcommand{\subfloat}[2][need a sub-caption]{\subcaptionbox{#1}{#2}}

\begin{document}

<<setup, echo = F, message = F, warning = F>>=
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = F, fig.align = 'center') # code chunks omitted by default
@

<<fig.cap = paste('Mean =', mean_a), eval.after = 'fig.cap', out.width = '.4\\linewidth'>>=
a <- rnorm(100)
mean_a <- mean(a)
plot(a)
@

<<fig.cap = 'Means', fig.subcap=c(paste('Mean =', mean_a), paste('Mean =', mean_b)), eval.after = 'fig.subcap', out.width = '.4\\linewidth'>>=
b <- rnorm(100)
mean_b <- mean(b)
plot(a)
plot(b)
@

\end{document}
```

title: Feature request: Support for CairoWin
description:
Being forced on Windows and needing to use the boss' Word templates I would like to use WMF/EMF files as output of my knitr Rmd documents so my Word documents have nicely scaling graphics. Recently I discovered the even nicer Cairo graphics but unfortunately knitr only supports base R's `win.metafile` device.

Based on the code in plot.R, it appears fairly easy to add support for CairoWin. See following patch. However, I am not sufficiently familiar with coding R packages as well as the internals of knitr to see whether other stuff needs to be changed or compile the package and test the changes.

diff --git a/R/plot.R b/R/plot.R

title: Equivalent of `--use-make` from `latexmk`
description:
Hi, 

Suppose i have a document that access external files when it is compiled through knitr. For exemple, suppose that my document contains :

- In the markdown part, `![](image.png)`
- In a R chunk, `data = read.csv("data.csv")`
- In a python chunk, `import pandas as pd` and then `other_data = pd.read_csv("other_data.csv")`

Then, when knitting my document to `output: html_document`, is it possible to tell knitr to behave like classical `make` for these files ? 

Indeed, i'm knitting my document from a makefile (for the moment using `R -e "pagedown::chrome_print('poster.Rmd')"`, but i'm willing to change that), and i have to explicitely tell the makefile that it depends on `data.csv`, `other_data.csv` and `image.png`. 

On the other hand, i know that `latexmk` has a `--use-make` option, which i already use when building latex documents, but here it's an html document. When encountering a file that is not up-to-date, `latexmk` ask the main `make` process to build the file and then continues to buil the pdf.

Can i achieve a similar behavior with knitr ?

Hi,

Starting with knitr 1.27 we started to see new vignette errors in several Bioconductor packages in release (BioC 3.10, based on R 3.6) and devel (BioC 3.11, based on R 4.0).

Here is how to reproduce:
 
1. Create a minimalist Rmd vignette that uses `knitr::include_graphics`:
    ```
    jpeg(file="myplot.jpeg")
    plot(1:10)
    rect(1, 5, 3, 7, col = "white")
    dev.off()

    Test_vignette.Rmd <- c(
        "---",
        "title: \"Test vignette\"",
        "---",
        "```{r chunk1}",
        "knitr::include_graphics(\"myplot.jpeg\")",
        "```")
    cat(Test_vignette.Rmd, sep="\n", file="Test_vignette.Rmd")
    ```

2. Rendering the vignette with `rmarkdown::html_document` works fine:
    ```
    library(rmarkdown)
    rmarkdown::render("Test_vignette.Rmd", rmarkdown::html_document())
    ```

3. Rendering the vignette with `rmarkdown::pdf_document` triggers a **non-fatal** error:
    ```
    rmarkdown::render("Test_vignette.Rmd", rmarkdown::pdf_document())
    ```
    Output:
    ```
    processing file: Test_vignette.Rmd
      |...................................                                   |  50%
      ordinary text without R code

      |......................................................................| 100%
    label: chunk1
    !!! Error: Input file `Test_vignette_files/figure-latex/chunk1-1.pdf' not found!

    output file: Test_vignette.knit.md

    /usr/bin/pandoc +RTS -K512m -RTS Test_vignette.utf8.md --to latex --from markdown+autolink_bare_uris+tex_math_single_backslash --output Test_vignette.tex --self-contained --highlight-style tango --pdf-engine pdflatex --variable graphics --lua-filter /home/biocbuild/bbs-3.10-bioc/R/library/rmarkdown/rmd/lua/pagebreak.lua --lua-filter /home/biocbuild/bbs-3.10-bioc/R/library/rmarkdown/rmd/lua/latex-div.lua --variable 'geometry:margin=1in' 

    Output created: Test_vignette.pdf
    ```

4. Trying to render the vignette again with `rmarkdown::html_document` after enabling cropping now produces a **fatal** error:

title: Don't overwrite input files specified in `knitr::include_graphics()`
description:
I also ran into #1797 after updating to knitr 1.27. Then I updated to the dev version (1.27.2) **and stumpled upon another issue** I'd call a bug, too:

It seems that **knitr is always overwriting the file included through `knitr::include_graphics()`**. I don't know if this was already the case before knitr 1.27. I noticed it because I tried to build an MVE for the original bug using knitr's reference card PDF vignette as follows:

```r
knitr::include_graphics(paste0(find.package(package = "knitr"), "/doc/knitr-refcard.pdf"))
```

Since I've installed knitr through Michael Rutter's PPA (Ubuntu Linux), on my system the above is equivalent to:

```r
knitr::include_graphics("/usr/lib/R/site-library/knitr/doc/knitr-refcard.pdf")
```

When I try to build this, the following error is thrown:

```
!!! Error: Cannot move `tmp-pdfcrop-6024.pdf' to `/usr/lib/R/site-library/knitr/doc/knitr-refcard.pdf'!
```

This is of course because knitr isn't run as root, but the file is owned by root and knitr doesn't have write permission:

```sh
$ ls -1l /usr/lib/R/site-library/knitr/doc/knitr-refcard.pdf
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 79531 Jan 19 04:04 /usr/lib/R/site-library/knitr/doc/knitr-refcard.pdf
```

I verified this with a file knitr actually has write permission to – it gets overwritten when included through `knitr::include_graphics()`! The documentation of `knitr::include_graphics()` doesn't say anything about possible file modifications of param `path` and I believe it was never really intended to overwrite `path`, right?

---

**Addendum:** I've just read about the `crop` option in #1796 and setting `knitr::opts_chunk$set(crop = NULL)` avoids knitr's attempt to overwrite the included PDF.

I think it's fine that knitr automatically crops white space around the files specified in `knitr::include_graphics()` **but it should still never overwrite the original files**!

~~And is there a specific reason why `crop` isn't a "proper" chunk options like e.g. `fig.path`?~~ @yihui 's [answer](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/1797#issuecomment-576809782):

> Because cropping images require additional software packages, and I tend to let users opt-in after they know how to install these packages, instead of "officially" supporting this feature.

---

title: problem with svg device, expression(), and unicode characters
description:
I am having difficulty using the `svg` device with math expressions and unicode (in this case, left- and right-quotes). This only occurs on my Windows 10 computer; my osx computer seems unaffected. Consider the following Rmardown document:

````
---
output: 
  html_document:
      dev: svg
---

```{r echo=FALSE}
plot(1, axes=FALSE, ty='n')

## Line A: 
 mtext(side = 2, text = expression(paste("A")))
## Line B:
 mtext(side = 3, text = expression(paste("“B")))
## Line C: 
 mtext(side = 4, text = expression(paste("C")))

axis(1, at = par()$usr[1:2], lab = c("More", "Less"), tick = FALSE)
```
````
(Note the left-quote in Line B). Compilation fails with the error:
```
Quitting from lines 8-18 (testing.Rmd) 
Error in mtext(side = 4, text = expression(paste("C"))) : 
  metric information not available for this device
Calls: <Anonymous> ... withCallingHandlers -> withVisible -> eval -> eval -> mtext
Execution halted
```

* If I change the device to `png` I get the output I expect.
* If I comment out lines B and C, I get the output I expect (eg, the output from lines A and the axis)
* If I comment out only line C, I do not get the output I expect. Neither line B works, nor the axis. There appears to be something wrong with line B that causes everything later in the chunk to fail too.
* If I remove the `expression()` from line B, everything works as expected (including the unicode left-quote)
* I tried installing the development version of `knitr` as the Issue Guide suggests, but that did not help.

This appears, then, to be an interaction between `svg`, `expression`, and unicode.

title: Figure and table references
description:
Currently, referencing figures and tables in knitr documents is a bit difficult. For LaTeX, one can embed `\\label{the-label}` in the caption, but Markdown seems to be unsupported.

I propose a solution that could work the same way with all backends. Example: The `kable` function would support an additional argument `label`, with different handling for different backends.
- Pandoc: `Table #:` is prepended to the caption, the number is associated with the label in some internal cache (where?)
- HTML: Similar
- LaTeX: `\\label{...}` is inserted in the caption

There'll also be a counterpart, a function `ref(label)`, that does the following:
- Pandoc and HTML: Write `Table #`
- LaTeX: Write `Table \\ref{...}` or `\\cref{...}`

It would be used in the following way in `.Rmd` documents:

```
`r ref("the-label")`
```

Similar considerations for figures.

Of course, for Pandoc and HTML, forward references will have to be handled by `knitr` itself. With a warning in case recompilation is required.

Thoughts?

title: showtext package integration
description:
## Description

When I try to knit Chinese into a PDF from Rmd, the Chinese can't be seen in the PDF. But the Chinese could be seen in html and doc with a warning. Then I loaded the `showtext` package, the warning disappeared in the html and doc but still no Chinese in PDF.  I referred to the log and found Rmd produce PDF for each picture, so I think the Rmd may use the PDF as default output device. If knitr could integrate the showtext package for the PDF device or define a new device for output, the user may feel free to use some font without considering the font or encode issues.
